title: Acne-Like Eruptions: When Pimples May Not Be Acne
seo_title: Acne-Like Eruptions | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Folliculitis, perioral dermatitis and hidradenitis can resemble acne. Learn the clues that make diagnosis important.
introduction: Not every group of bumps is acne. Folliculitis, perioral dermatitis, rosacea, hidradenitis suppurativa and product reactions can look acne-like but require different treatment.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: Not every group of bumps is acne. Folliculitis, perioral dermatitis, rosacea, hidradenitis suppurativa and product reactions can look acne-like but require different treatment.

value.heading: Which conditions commonly resemble acne?
value.body:
The pattern, body area, symptoms and presence or absence of comedones help narrow the diagnosis.

  • Folliculitis: follicle-centred bumps that may itch or follow sweating, shaving or infection
  • Perioral dermatitis: small bumps and irritation around the mouth, nose or eyes
  • Rosacea: facial flushing, sensitivity and inflammatory bumps without typical blackheads
  • Hidradenitis suppurativa: recurrent painful deep lumps in folds such as the armpits or groin
  • Steroid-related or cosmetic-product eruptions: sudden uniform bumps after a trigger

value.heading: What clues suggest it may not be ordinary acne?
value.body:
Severe itching, burning, flushing, identical-looking bumps, unusual body sites, recurrent boils in skin folds or worsening after steroid cream are reasons to reconsider the diagnosis.

Acne can coexist with another condition, so a mixed pattern is also possible.

value.heading: Why does the correct diagnosis matter?
value.body:
Using routine acne products on perioral dermatitis or sensitive rosacea can increase irritation. Repeatedly treating hidradenitis as isolated pimples can delay care and allow scarring or tunnels to develop.

A clinician may review medicines, steroid use, shaving, sweating, cosmetics, menstrual symptoms and lesion distribution before selecting treatment.

value.heading: When should an acne-like rash be assessed promptly?
value.body: Prompt review is appropriate for fever, rapidly spreading redness, severe pain, lesions close to the eye, recurrent draining lumps, scarring in body folds or sudden widespread eruption after a medicine.

items.question: Can folliculitis be mistaken for acne?
items.answer: Yes. Folliculitis can create acne-like follicular bumps, but the cause and treatment may differ.

items.question: Does rosacea cause blackheads?
items.answer: Typical rosacea does not usually produce blackheads or whiteheads. Their presence may suggest acne as well as, or instead of, rosacea.

items.question: What is the first sign of hidradenitis suppurativa?
items.answer: It can begin as a tender deep lump in an armpit, groin, buttock or inner thigh and may be mistaken for a boil or acne cyst.

title: Painful Acne Nodules: Why Early Treatment Matters
seo_title: Painful Acne Nodules | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Painful acne nodules are deep inflammatory lesions with a higher scarring risk. Learn when dermatologist care is important.
introduction: Acne nodules are deep, firm and often painful inflammatory lesions. Unlike surface pimples, they develop deeper in the skin and carry a greater risk of permanent scarring.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: Acne nodules are deep, firm and often painful inflammatory lesions. Unlike surface pimples, they develop deeper in the skin and carry a greater risk of permanent scarring.

value.heading: How is an acne nodule different from a pimple?
value.body:
A nodule is usually larger, firmer and deeper than a papule or pustule. It may not have a visible head and can remain tender for days or weeks.

Several deep lesions may be described as nodular acne and warrant timely medical assessment.

value.heading: Why do nodules need early attention?
value.body:
Deep inflammation can damage surrounding collagen and increase the risk of depressed or raised scars.

  • Pain and swelling can interfere with sleep or daily activity
  • Picking or attempted drainage can worsen tissue injury
  • New lesions may continue while older nodules are healing
  • Lingering dark or red marks are common after inflammation

value.heading: How may nodular acne be treated?
value.body:
A dermatologist assesses severity, distribution, scarring, previous medicines, medical history and pregnancy considerations. Deep acne often needs a prescription plan and monitoring rather than spot treatment alone.

Selected individual lesions may sometimes receive an in-clinic treatment, but the wider goal is to prevent new nodules.

value.heading: When is urgent review needed?
value.body: Prompt review is appropriate for rapidly worsening pain, widespread deep acne, scarring, emotional distress or a lesion that may instead be an abscess. Fever or spreading redness needs urgent medical attention.

items.question: Can a painful nodule be drained at home?
items.answer: No. Home puncture or squeezing can worsen inflammation, infection and scarring. A clinician should confirm what the lesion is before any procedure.

items.question: Do acne nodules always scar?
items.answer: Not every nodule causes a permanent scar, but the risk is higher than with superficial acne. Early control and avoiding picking may reduce risk.

items.question: Is a nodule the same as a cyst?
items.answer: The terms are sometimes used together in everyday language, but dermatologists distinguish lesions by their clinical features. Both deep painful patterns deserve assessment.

title: Small Red Pimples: Understanding Acne Papules
seo_title: Small Red Pimples | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Small red pimples may be acne papules or another rash. Learn the signs, safe care and when assessment is needed in Jammu.
introduction: Acne papules are small, raised, inflamed bumps that usually look red, pink, brown or purple depending on skin tone. They do not have a visible pus-filled centre.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: Acne papules are small, raised, inflamed bumps that usually look red, pink, brown or purple depending on skin tone. They do not have a visible pus-filled centre.

value.heading: What causes acne papules?
value.body:
A blocked follicle can become inflamed, producing a tender raised bump. Papules may develop alongside blackheads, whiteheads and pustules.

The colour of inflammation varies across skin tones, so acne severity should not be judged by redness alone.

value.heading: Why should papules not be picked?
value.body:
Picking can push inflammation deeper, delay healing and increase the chance of a dark mark or permanent scar.

  • Avoid needles, pinching and abrasive spot tools
  • Use gentle cleansing rather than repeated scrubbing
  • Keep hair and pore-blocking products away from acne-prone areas
  • Follow prescribed treatment consistently rather than only treating visible spots

value.heading: Could a red bump be something other than acne?
value.body: Yes. Folliculitis, rosacea, perioral dermatitis, insect bites and product irritation can all produce red bumps. Itching, a sudden uniform eruption, unusual distribution or lack of comedones may suggest another diagnosis.

value.heading: When should inflamed acne be treated medically?
value.body: Dermatology review is useful when papules are numerous, painful, recurrent, leaving marks or spreading to the chest and back. Early control may reduce the risk of progression and scarring.

items.question: What is the difference between a papule and a pustule?
items.answer: A papule is an inflamed solid bump without visible pus. A pustule has a pale or yellow pus-filled centre.

items.question: Can papules turn into deeper acne?
items.answer: Some inflamed lesions can become larger or deeper. Worsening tenderness, size or number is a reason to review the treatment plan.

items.question: Will every red pimple leave a mark?
items.answer: No, but inflammation, picking and deeper skin tones can increase the likelihood of lingering colour change.

title: Pus-Filled Pimples: Acne Pustules Explained
seo_title: Pus-Filled Pimples | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Understand acne pustules, why pus-filled pimples develop and when recurring or painful lesions need dermatologist assessment.
introduction: An acne pustule is an inflamed pimple with a visible white or yellow centre. It forms when inflammation and immune cells collect within a blocked follicle.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: An acne pustule is an inflamed pimple with a visible white or yellow centre. It forms when inflammation and immune cells collect within a blocked follicle.

value.heading: What does an acne pustule look like?
value.body:
A pustule is usually a small raised lesion with a pale centre and an inflamed base. It may feel tender and can occur with comedones or deeper acne.

Large, rapidly worsening or very painful pus-filled lesions may represent a boil, abscess or another infection rather than routine acne.

value.heading: Why is popping a pustule risky?
value.body:
Popping can spread inflammation into surrounding tissue and increases trauma to the follicle.

  • More swelling and tenderness
  • Post-inflammatory dark or red marks
  • Secondary infection
  • A higher chance of textural scarring

value.heading: How are recurrent pustules assessed?
value.body:
The distribution, presence of blackheads or whiteheads, use of steroids or cosmetics, shaving pattern and medication history help distinguish acne from folliculitis and other eruptions.

Treatment is selected according to the full acne pattern rather than the colour of one spot. Repeated antibiotics without an overall plan may not provide durable control.

value.heading: Which warning signs need prompt care?
value.body: Seek prompt medical advice for spreading redness, fever, severe pain, rapidly enlarging swelling, lesions near the eye or a soft fluctuant lump that may be an abscess.

items.question: Does pus always mean infection?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Acne pustules contain inflammatory material within a follicle, but a boil or abscess is a different problem and may need urgent treatment.

items.question: Can acne pustules leave scars?
items.answer: They can leave colour changes, while deeper or repeatedly traumatised lesions have a greater risk of permanent scarring.

items.question: Should an antibiotic cream be used on every pustule?
items.answer: No. Unsupervised antibiotic use can be ineffective and contributes to resistance. Acne treatment should follow an appropriate diagnosis and complete plan.

title: Blackheads: Causes, Care and When to See a Dermatologist
seo_title: Blackheads | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Understand why blackheads form, what can make them worse and when to seek dermatologist-led acne care in Jammu.
introduction: Blackheads are open comedones: small blocked pores whose contents are exposed at the skin surface. The dark colour is caused by oxidation, not trapped dirt, so harsh scrubbing is not the answer.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: Blackheads are open comedones: small blocked pores whose contents are exposed at the skin surface. The dark colour is caused by oxidation, not trapped dirt, so harsh scrubbing is not the answer.

value.heading: What exactly is a blackhead?
value.body:
A blackhead develops when oil and dead skin cells collect inside a hair follicle. Because the pore remains open, the material at the surface reacts with air and looks brown or black.

Blackheads are common on the nose, forehead, chin, chest and back. They may occur alone or alongside whiteheads, inflamed pimples and oily skin.

value.heading: What can make blackheads worse?
value.body:
Blackheads are influenced by oil production, pore blockage and acne tendency. They are not proof that the skin is dirty.

  • Heavy or pore-blocking skin and hair products
  • Picking, squeezing or repeated metal-tool extraction
  • Aggressive scrubs that irritate the skin barrier
  • Stopping an effective acne routine too early
  • Hormonal changes that increase oil production

value.heading: How are blackheads managed?
value.body:
A dermatologist first confirms that the dark dots are comedones rather than normal sebaceous filaments, enlarged pores or another condition. A plan may include suitable topical acne treatment, gentle non-comedogenic skin care and medically supervised extraction for selected lesions.

Improvement is gradual. A maintenance plan is often needed because pores can block again even after successful extraction.

value.heading: When should blackheads be examined?
value.body: Arrange an assessment if blackheads are widespread, repeatedly inflamed, leaving marks, occurring with painful acne or not improving despite consistent care. Sudden severe acne in adulthood or acne with hormonal symptoms may need a broader review.

value.body:

items.question: Can blackheads be permanently removed?
items.answer: Individual blackheads can clear, but new ones can form because oil production and pore blockage may continue. Ongoing maintenance is usually more realistic than a permanent one-time removal.

items.question: Should I squeeze blackheads at home?
items.answer: Squeezing can cause inflammation, infection, marks or scarring. Medically supervised extraction is safer for selected lesions and should be part of a wider acne plan.

items.question: Are nose dots always blackheads?
items.answer: No. Sebaceous filaments are normal structures that can look like small grey dots, especially on the nose. Examination helps distinguish them from true open comedones.

title: Deep Cystic Acne: Symptoms, Risks and Treatment Planning
seo_title: Deep Cystic Acne | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Deep cystic acne can be painful and scar. Learn why diagnosis-led treatment and follow-up matter for severe breakouts.
introduction: Cystic acne describes deep, painful inflammatory breakouts that may feel soft or fluctuant beneath the skin. Severe deep acne should be assessed early because delayed control can lead to lasting scars.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: Cystic acne describes deep, painful inflammatory breakouts that may feel soft or fluctuant beneath the skin. Severe deep acne should be assessed early because delayed control can lead to lasting scars.

value.heading: What are the signs of deep cystic acne?
value.body:
Lesions are usually larger than ordinary pimples, sit deep in the skin and may remain painful for a prolonged period. They can occur on the face, jaw, neck, chest, shoulders or back.

Deep acne may occur with nodules, inflamed pustules, comedones and existing scars.

value.heading: What increases the risk of scarring?
value.body:
Depth and duration of inflammation matter. Repeated squeezing, delayed treatment and continuing new lesions add further risk.

  • Multiple deep lesions
  • A personal or family tendency to acne scars
  • Picking, puncturing or aggressive facials
  • Uncontrolled acne over several months
  • Breakouts on the chest, shoulders or back

value.heading: How is cystic acne treatment planned?
value.body:
The plan depends on severity, age, medical history, previous response and pregnancy potential. Prescription oral and topical treatment may be considered, with counselling and monitoring appropriate to the medicine selected.

Scar procedures are generally planned after active acne is controlled so that new damage is not continuing during scar treatment.

value.heading: Could a deep lump be something else?
value.body: Yes. Boils, abscesses, inflamed cysts and hidradenitis suppurativa can resemble cystic acne. A hot, rapidly expanding, fluctuant or fever-associated lump requires prompt assessment.

value.body:

items.question: Can cystic acne be treated with facials alone?
items.answer: No. Facials do not replace medical treatment for deep inflammatory acne and aggressive manipulation can worsen painful lesions.

items.question: When is isotretinoin considered?
items.answer: A dermatologist may consider isotretinoin for selected severe, scarring or treatment-resistant acne. It requires careful supervision and strict pregnancy-prevention measures where relevant.

items.question: Should scar treatment start immediately?
items.answer: Active acne is usually controlled first. Once new deep lesions are reduced, scar type and suitable procedures can be assessed separately.

title: Oily Skin and Acne: A Practical Skin-Care Guide
seo_title: Oily Skin and Acne | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Oily skin does not need harsh scrubbing. Learn gentle, non-comedogenic care and when persistent acne needs assessment.
eyebrow: Acne skin care · Medical review pending
introduction: Oily skin occurs when sebaceous glands produce more surface oil. It can accompany acne, but stripping the skin with harsh cleansers may increase irritation without solving blocked pores.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: Oily skin occurs when sebaceous glands produce more surface oil. It can accompany acne, but stripping the skin with harsh cleansers may increase irritation without solving blocked pores.

value.heading: Does oily skin always mean acne?
value.body:
No. Some people have oily skin without acne, while others develop acne because oil combines with follicular blockage and inflammation.

A shiny face alone is not a reason to use several strong active ingredients at once.

value.heading: What is a sensible routine for oily acne-prone skin?
value.body:
A simple routine is easier to tolerate and follow consistently.

  • Cleanse gently up to twice daily and after heavy sweating
  • Choose oil-free or non-comedogenic products
  • Use a lightweight moisturiser if treatment causes dryness
  • Apply suitable broad-spectrum sunscreen
  • Avoid alcohol-heavy astringents and abrasive scrubbing
  • Keep oily hair products away from acne-prone facial skin

value.heading: Why can over-cleansing make things worse?
value.body:
Frequent washing, hot water and scrubbing can disrupt the skin barrier, causing stinging, redness and poor tolerance of acne medicines. Irritated skin can look shinier and more inflamed.

Oil control should not come at the cost of barrier damage.

value.heading: When should oily skin be assessed?
value.body: Seek advice when oiliness is accompanied by persistent comedones, inflamed acne, scarring, sudden adult-onset symptoms or irritation from multiple products. A clinician can simplify the routine and select treatment for the actual acne type.

items.question: Should oily skin skip moisturiser?
items.answer: Not always. Acne treatment can dry or irritate the skin, and a suitable non-comedogenic moisturiser can improve comfort and adherence.

items.question: How often should oily skin be washed?
items.answer: Gentle cleansing up to twice daily and after sweating is usually sufficient. More frequent washing can irritate the skin.

items.question: Can sunscreen worsen oily skin?
items.answer: A product that feels heavy may be uncomfortable, but sunscreen remains important. Look for a non-comedogenic formula suited to oily skin.

title: Post-Acne Dark Marks: Understanding PIH
seo_title: Post-Acne Dark Marks | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation can leave flat brown or grey marks after acne. Learn prevention and treatment planning.
introduction: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) is a flat brown, grey-brown or dark mark that remains after acne inflammation. It is especially common and noticeable in medium-to-deep skin tones.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) is a flat brown, grey-brown or dark mark that remains after acne inflammation. It is especially common and noticeable in medium-to-deep skin tones.

value.heading: Is a dark acne mark the same as a scar?
value.body:
No. PIH changes colour but does not create a pit or raised area. A scar involves a lasting change in skin texture.

A person can have active acne, PIH and textural scars at the same time, so each component should be identified.

value.heading: Why do dark marks keep appearing?
value.body:
Every new inflamed lesion can trigger more pigment. Picking and irritating skin care can deepen the colour.

  • Uncontrolled inflammatory acne
  • Squeezing, scratching or home extraction
  • Harsh peels or unprescribed steroid-mixed creams
  • Sun exposure without suitable protection
  • Skin-barrier irritation from too many active ingredients

value.heading: How is PIH managed?
value.body:
Preventing new acne is central. A dermatologist may combine acne control, gentle skin care, suitable sunscreen and selected pigment treatment according to skin type and sensitivity.

Chemical peels or laser procedures are not automatically appropriate for every dark mark. Incorrect settings or excessive treatment can worsen pigmentation.

value.heading: How long do dark marks take to fade?
value.body: Fading can take months and deeper colour may persist longer. Improvement depends on pigment depth, ongoing acne, sun exposure and treatment tolerance; instant clearing should not be promised.

items.question: Can sunscreen help acne dark marks?
items.answer: Sun protection helps prevent existing pigment from becoming more noticeable and supports a broader treatment plan.

items.question: Will bleaching cream remove every mark?
items.answer: No. Unsupervised strong products can irritate skin and worsen PIH. Treatment should match the type and depth of pigmentation.

items.question: Can PIH occur without acne scars?
items.answer: Yes. A flat dark mark can remain even when the skin texture is normal.

title: Post-Acne Red Marks: How They Differ from Scars
seo_title: Post-Acne Red Marks | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Flat red or pink marks after acne are not always scars. Learn why they occur, how they fade and when treatment may help.
introduction: A flat pink, red or purple area left after a pimple may be a post-inflammatory colour change rather than a permanent textural scar. These marks can fade, but continued breakouts create new ones.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: A flat pink, red or purple area left after a pimple may be a post-inflammatory colour change rather than a permanent textural scar. These marks can fade, but continued breakouts create new ones.

value.heading: What causes red marks after acne?
value.body:
Inflammation can leave temporary changes in small surface blood vessels and skin colour after the active lesion settles. The appearance varies with skin tone and the depth of the original inflammation.

A mark is flat. An acne scar changes the skin surface by creating a depression or raised area.

value.heading: What can make red marks last longer?
value.body:
Ongoing acne, picking, irritation and unprotected sun exposure can prolong uneven colour.

  • Squeezing or scratching healing lesions
  • Using harsh acids or scrubs on irritated skin
  • Skipping acne maintenance
  • Confusing redness with a scar and choosing the wrong procedure

value.heading: How are post-acne red marks managed?
value.body:
The first priority is controlling active acne and preventing further inflammation. Gentle skin care and sunscreen support recovery.

If marks remain troublesome, a dermatologist can confirm whether the main issue is vascular redness, brown pigmentation, mixed colour or textural scarring before discussing procedures.

value.heading: When should a mark be examined?
value.body: Assessment is helpful when marks are persistent, mixed with scars, associated with ongoing painful acne or worsening despite appropriate care. A spot that bleeds, crusts or changes independently of acne needs diagnosis.

items.question: Are red acne marks permanent?
items.answer: Many flat colour changes fade gradually, but the timeline varies. A true textural scar does not disappear simply because its colour settles.

items.question: Can red marks and dark marks occur together?
items.answer: Yes. Mixed red, purple and brown changes are common, especially across different skin tones and stages of healing.

items.question: Should laser be used for every red mark?
items.answer: No. The type of colour change, skin type, active acne and risk of post-inflammatory pigmentation must be assessed first.

title: Whiteheads: Closed Comedones and Acne Care
seo_title: Whiteheads | Aastha Skin Jammu
search_description: Learn what whiteheads are, why closed comedones develop and how dermatologist-led acne care is planned in Jammu.
introduction: Whiteheads are closed comedones—small flesh-coloured or pale bumps caused by a blocked follicle whose surface opening has closed. They are different from pus-filled pimples and should not be repeatedly squeezed.

value.heading: Key point
value.body: Whiteheads are closed comedones—small flesh-coloured or pale bumps caused by a blocked follicle whose surface opening has closed. They are different from pus-filled pimples and should not be repeatedly squeezed.

value.heading: How do whiteheads form?
value.body:
Oil and dead skin cells collect inside a follicle. When the opening stays covered by a thin layer of skin, the blockage appears as a small raised bump rather than a dark open comedone.

Whiteheads can occur on the forehead, cheeks, chin, jaw, chest and back. Clusters may make the skin feel rough even when there is little redness.

value.heading: What may look like a whitehead?
value.body:
Not every pale bump is acne. Milia, folliculitis, irritation, keratosis pilaris and some cosmetic-product reactions can resemble closed comedones.

  • Milia are tiny keratin cysts and need a different approach
  • Folliculitis often centres on hair follicles and may itch
  • Perioral dermatitis commonly clusters around the mouth or nose
  • Inflamed pustules contain visible pus and are not simple whiteheads

value.heading: How are whiteheads treated?
value.body:
Treatment aims to prevent follicles from blocking and to control any accompanying inflammation. Depending on age, skin sensitivity, pregnancy considerations and acne severity, a dermatologist may recommend topical medicines, selected procedures or changes to pore-blocking products.

Scrubs and frequent extraction alone do not address why new comedones form. Consistent treatment usually matters more than aggressive cleaning.

value.heading: When is medical review useful?
value.body: Seek assessment when bumps are persistent, spreading, becoming inflamed, leaving marks or not responding to appropriate over-the-counter care. Review is also useful when the diagnosis is uncertain.

items.question: Are whiteheads filled with pus?
items.answer: No. A whitehead is a closed follicular blockage. A pustule is an inflamed acne lesion with visible pus and usually has surrounding redness.

items.question: Can moisturiser cause whiteheads?
items.answer: Some heavy products may contribute to clogged pores, but moisturiser itself is not automatically harmful. Choose products labelled oil-free or non-comedogenic and suited to your skin.

items.question: How quickly do whiteheads clear?
items.answer: The timeline varies with the number of lesions, treatment used and consistency. Acne treatment usually needs several weeks before its full response can be judged.

value.heading: Personalised treatment for rolling, boxcar and ice-pick acne scars
value.body:
Consult Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist, for diagnosis-led acne scar treatment at Aastha Skin & Dermato-Cosmetic Centre in Jammu.

Acne scars do not all behave in the same way. Treatment is planned after assessing the scar type, depth, skin tone, active acne, pigmentation tendency and acceptable downtime.

Acne scar procedures, MNRF and fractional CO₂ laser are available at both the Karan Nagar and Paloura branches.

value.heading: When should acne scar treatment begin?
value.body:
Scar treatment usually begins after active acne is reasonably controlled. Continuing breakouts can create new scars while older scars are being treated.

Patients may be advised to continue acne medication or maintenance skincare during their scar-treatment course.

A consultation is especially useful when:

  • Scars are becoming more noticeable
  • Acne has left deep pits or uneven texture
  • Makeup does not sit evenly on the skin
  • Scarring affects confidence
  • Previous treatments produced limited improvement
  • Dark marks and textural scars are present together

The patient has a history of keloids

Active acne is still recurring

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
What are acne scars?

Acne scars are permanent changes in skin texture that remain after acne inflammation has healed. They commonly develop after deep nodules or cysts, and the risk can increase when pimples are picked, scratched or squeezed.

Acne scars may be:

  • Depressed below the skin surface
  • Raised above the surrounding skin
  • Narrow and deep
  • Broad and shallow
  • Tethered to deeper tissue
  • Associated with redness or pigmentation

Dark or red marks left after acne are not always true scars. They may represent post-inflammatory colour changes without permanent textural damage.

Ice-pick scars

Ice-pick scars are narrow but extend deeply into the skin. They often look like small holes or punctures.

Boxcar scars

Boxcar scars are round or oval depressions with more clearly defined edges. They may be shallow or deep.

Rolling scars

Rolling scars are broad, shallow depressions that can give the skin a wavy appearance. Some are held down by fibrous bands beneath the skin.

Hypertrophic scars

Hypertrophic scars are raised, firm scars caused by excessive collagen formation. They commonly remain within the original area of inflammation.

Keloid scars

Keloids are raised scars that may extend beyond the original acne lesion. Raised scars require a different approach from depressed scars.

Many patients have more than one scar type, which is why a combination treatment plan may be recommended.

Acne marks

Acne marks are changes in colour left after inflammation. They may appear:

  • Brown
  • Grey-brown
  • Red
  • Pink
  • Purple

The skin surface usually remains smooth.

Acne scars

Acne scars cause a lasting change in texture. The skin may look depressed, pitted, wavy or raised.

Pigmentation treatment cannot lift a deep scar, while resurfacing alone may not completely correct dark marks. Each concern should therefore be assessed separately.

How does Dr. Cheena Langer assess acne scars?

An acne scar consultation may include:

  • Identifying each scar type
  • Assessing scar depth and distribution
  • Checking whether scars are tethered
  • Looking for active acne
  • Evaluating pigmentation and redness
  • Reviewing skin tone and sensitivity
  • Asking about previous procedures
  • Assessing keloid tendency
  • Discussing recovery time and expectations
  • Preparing a staged treatment plan

The dermatologist also considers age, scar duration, medical history, budget and the amount of downtime the patient can manage.

Which acne scar treatments may be considered?

Acne scar treatment is rarely one-size-fits-all. Dermatologists may use more than one technique because different scar types respond differently.

Possible options include:

  • MNRF
  • Microneedling
  • Subcision
  • Fractional CO₂ laser
  • Focal treatment for selected deep scars
  • Chemical peels for associated pigmentation
  • PRP-supported procedures
  • Scar revision in selected cases
  • Combination treatment plans

The appropriate option depends on the scar pattern and individual skin assessment.

What is MNRF for acne scars?

MNRF stands for microneedling radiofrequency. Fine needles deliver controlled radiofrequency energy into selected skin depths to support collagen remodelling.

MNRF may be considered for:

  • Rolling scars
  • Selected boxcar scars
  • Uneven skin texture
  • Enlarged pores
  • Mixed atrophic acne scars

Radiofrequency microneedling has evidence supporting its use for acne scarring, although treatment settings, study methods and results vary. Further high-quality studies are still needed to define ideal protocols.

Temporary effects can include:

  • Redness
  • Mild swelling
  • Tenderness
  • Pinpoint crusting
  • Temporary sensitivity
  • Short-term darkening in some patients

Several sessions may be recommended depending on scar severity and response.

What is fractional CO₂ laser for acne scars?

Fractional CO₂ laser creates controlled microscopic treatment zones in the skin. Healing and collagen remodelling can gradually make selected depressed scars less noticeable.

It may be considered for:

  • Boxcar scars
  • Mixed atrophic scars
  • Uneven texture
  • Selected rolling scars
  • Certain surgical or chickenpox scars

Recovery may involve:

  • Redness
  • Swelling
  • Crusting
  • Peeling
  • Temporary sensitivity
  • Post-inflammatory pigmentation

Recent comparative reviews indicate that fractional CO₂ laser and needling-based treatments can both improve atrophic acne scars. Fractional CO₂ may provide stronger improvement in some comparisons but can carry a higher risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and longer recovery, making skin type and individual risk important considerations.

Individual scar assessment

Treatment is chosen according to scar type, depth and skin tone rather than offering one procedure to every patient.

Active acne and scar care together

New breakouts are addressed to reduce the risk of additional scars.

items.question: What is subcision?
items.answer:
Subcision is a minor procedure used for selected depressed scars that are pulled down by fibrous bands beneath the skin.

A fine needle or suitable instrument is passed under the scar to release the tethering. Once released, the depressed area may rise and collagen remodelling can occur during healing.

Subcision is most often considered for:

  • Rolling scars
  • Tethered depressions
  • Broad, sunken scars
  • Scars that become smoother when the surrounding skin is stretched

It may be combined with microneedling, MNRF, laser or another scar procedure when appropriate. The AAD describes surgical lifting or release of depressed scars as one of the procedural approaches dermatologists may use.

items.question: What is microneedling?
items.answer:
Microneedling uses fine sterile needles to create controlled micro-injuries in the skin. This stimulates healing processes and collagen production that may gradually reduce the appearance of selected depressed scars.

It may be used alone or combined with:

  • Radiofrequency
  • PRP
  • Chemical peeling
  • Subcision
  • Other scar procedures

The American Academy of Dermatology notes that microneedling is used for depressed acne scars and can be combined with radiofrequency or PRP.

items.question: Can PRP be combined with acne scar treatment?
items.answer:
Platelet-rich plasma, or PRP, may be used as a supportive treatment alongside procedures such as microneedling.

PRP is prepared from the patient’s own blood and contains platelets and associated growth factors. It is generally used to support healing rather than as a stand-alone answer for every scar type.

Its suitability depends on the main procedure, skin condition, medical history and treatment plan.

items.question: Can chemical peels treat acne scars?
items.answer:
Chemical peels may help with:

  • Post-acne pigmentation
  • Mild textural irregularity
  • Comedonal acne
  • Superficial skin roughness
  • Selected shallow scars

They are less likely to correct deep, tethered scars when used alone.

Peel type and strength should be selected according to skin tone, active acne, sensitivity and pigmentation risk.

items.question: Why are combination treatments often used?
items.answer:
A patient may have rolling scars, boxcar scars, ice-pick scars and pigmentation at the same time. One procedure cannot address every component equally.

A staged plan may therefore involve:

  • Subcision for tethered rolling scars
  • MNRF for collagen remodelling
  • Fractional CO₂ for selected texture concerns
  • Focal treatment for narrow deep scars
  • Peels or skincare for pigmentation
  • Continued acne control to prevent new scars

The AAD notes that dermatologists often combine treatments to address different scar patterns and improve overall results.

items.question: How many sessions are needed?
items.answer:
The number of sessions depends on:

  • Scar type
  • Scar depth
  • Treatment selected
  • Skin response
  • Previous procedures
  • Downtime available
  • Pigmentation tendency
  • Desired degree of improvement

Acne scar treatment is rarely completed in one session. Some patients require three or more sessions, and collagen improvement may continue gradually after treatment.

The final session plan should be given only after examination.

items.question: Can acne scars be removed completely?
items.answer:
Treatment can make acne scars less noticeable, improve texture and soften sharp transitions between scarred and normal skin.

Complete scar removal cannot be guaranteed. Results vary according to scar type, depth, skin tone, healing response and adherence to aftercare.

The goal is realistic, progressive improvement rather than perfectly unscarred skin.

value.heading: What is acne?
value.body:
Acne is an inflammatory condition involving blocked hair follicles, oil production and inflammation. It may appear as blackheads, whiteheads, red pimples, pus-filled spots, painful nodules or cysts.

Acne commonly affects teenagers and young adults, but it can continue into adulthood or begin for the first time later in life. It may affect confidence and emotional wellbeing as well as the skin.

value.heading: Common signs of acne
value.body:
• Blackheads
  • Whiteheads
  • Small red pimples
  • Pus-filled lesions
  • Painful nodules
  • Deep cystic breakouts
  • Oily skin
  • Post-acne red marks
  • Post-acne dark marks
  • Acne scars

Not every acne-like eruption is acne. Folliculitis, perioral dermatitis and hidradenitis suppurativa can resemble acne but require different treatment.

value.heading: What causes acne?
value.body:
Acne develops through a combination of blocked follicles, excess oil, inflammation and changes in organisms normally present on the skin. Hormonal activity and genetic tendency can also influence its development.

Factors that may contribute to acne or worsen breakouts include:

  • Hormonal changes
  • Family history
  • Oily or pore-blocking products
  • Friction from helmets, masks or tight clothing
  • Certain medicines
  • Stress-related worsening
  • Picking or squeezing lesions
  • Unsuitable skincare
  • Stopping treatment too early

Acne is not simply caused by poor hygiene. Aggressive scrubbing can irritate the skin and may make inflammation worse.

value.heading: When should acne be examined by a dermatologist?
value.body:
Consider a dermatology consultation when acne:

  • Is painful or deep
  • Is leaving scars
  • Causes persistent dark marks
  • Affects the chest or back extensively
  • Does not improve with basic care
  • Keeps returning
  • Begins suddenly in adulthood
  • Causes emotional distress
  • Is associated with irregular periods or unwanted hair growth
  • Is being treated repeatedly with antibiotics without lasting control
  • Appears different from typical acne

NICE guidance recognises the importance of acne severity, scarring, treatment response and the condition’s psychological effect when planning care or considering specialist referral.

value.heading: How does Dr. Cheena Langer assess acne?
value.body:
An acne consultation may include:

  • Examining the type and distribution of lesions
  • Assessing acne severity
  • Checking for marks and scars
  • Reviewing previous medicines and products
  • Asking about menstrual or hormonal symptoms where relevant
  • Reviewing current medicines and medical history
  • Identifying irritation caused by skincare
  • Discussing the effect of acne on confidence and daily life
  • Planning active treatment and maintenance

Tests are not required for every patient. Blood tests or hormonal assessment may be considered when the history or examination suggests an underlying issue.

value.heading: How is acne treated?
value.body: There is no single treatment that is suitable for everyone. Treatment depends on acne type, severity, body area, age, pregnancy considerations, previous response and tendency to develop scars.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Comedonal acne

Comedonal acne mainly causes blackheads and whiteheads because pores become blocked.

Inflammatory acne

Inflammatory acne causes red, tender or pus-filled pimples.

Nodular or cystic acne

Deep nodules and cysts can be painful and have a higher risk of permanent scarring.

Teenage acne

Acne commonly develops around puberty because hormonal changes affect oil production.

Adult acne

Acne may persist into adulthood or begin later, particularly around the lower face, jawline and chin.

Hormonal-pattern acne

Breakouts may follow a cyclical pattern or be associated with other hormonal symptoms. Medical evaluation may be needed when acne occurs with irregular periods, increased facial hair or scalp thinning.

Body acne

Acne may affect the back, chest, shoulders and upper arms as well as the face.

Acne with marks or scars

Dark marks and red marks are colour changes after inflammation. They are different from permanent textural scars.

Prescription topical treatment

Topical medicines may be used to:

  • Unblock pores
  • Reduce inflammation
  • Control acne-causing organisms
  • Prevent new lesions
  • Improve post-acne pigmentation

Current acne guidelines support several topical treatment classes and often favour combinations that work through different mechanisms.

Oral treatment

Oral medicines may be considered for moderate, severe, widespread or treatment-resistant acne.

Options depend on the patient’s age, medical history, pregnancy potential, acne severity and previous response. Systemic antibiotics should be used carefully and generally alongside appropriate topical treatment rather than as indefinite stand-alone therapy.

Oral isotretinoin

Oral isotretinoin may be considered for selected patients with severe acne, acne at high risk of permanent scarring or acne that has not responded adequately to appropriate treatment.

It requires careful medical supervision, counselling, monitoring and strict pregnancy-prevention measures where relevant. NICE updated its isotretinoin recommendations in April 2026 to reflect current risk-minimisation requirements.

Chemical peels

Selected medical chemical peels may support treatment for comedonal acne, oily skin and post-acne pigmentation.

The peel type and strength must be chosen according to skin type, active inflammation, sensitivity and current medicines.

Comedone management

Selected blackheads and whiteheads may be treated through medically supervised extraction as part of a broader acne plan.

Treatment for painful individual lesions

A dermatologist may consider an in-clinic injection for selected large, painful inflammatory lesions when clinically appropriate. Current acne guidance recognises intralesional corticosteroid treatment as an adjunctive option for appropriate individual lesions.

How long does acne treatment take?

Acne generally improves gradually rather than overnight. The skin needs time to respond, and early dryness or irritation can occur with some medicines.

A treatment review is usually needed to assess:

  • Reduction in new breakouts
  • Tolerance of medicines
  • Adherence to the routine
  • New marks or scars
  • Need for dose or product changes
  • Whether maintenance treatment is required

Patients should not stop treatment immediately after the skin begins to improve. Maintenance therapy may help reduce relapse, and NICE acne guidance includes specific recommendations for recurrence and maintenance.

Can acne be cured permanently?

Acne can often be controlled effectively, but recurrence is possible because hormonal activity, genetics and skin behaviour may continue.

The aim of treatment is to:

  • Control active acne
  • Reduce the frequency and severity of breakouts
  • Prevent scars
  • Reduce marks
  • Maintain improvement

Claims of an instant or guaranteed permanent cure should be avoided.

Acne marks

Acne marks are changes in skin colour after a breakout. They may appear:

  • Brown or dark
  • Red or pink
  • Purple-grey in deeper skin tones

These marks may gradually fade, although treatment and sun protection can help.

Acne scars

Acne scars involve a permanent change in skin texture.

They may be:

  • Ice-pick scars
  • Boxcar scars
  • Rolling scars
  • Raised scars
  • Keloids

Different scar types require different treatments. A scar plan should be based on examination rather than one standard procedure for every patient.

Why should active acne be controlled before scar treatment?

Continuing breakouts can produce new scars even while older scars are being treated. Dermatologists therefore commonly begin by controlling active acne and preventing new lesions before starting intensive scar procedures.

Once acne is controlled, a separate scar assessment may consider:

  • MNRF
  • Microneedling
  • Subcision
  • TCA CROSS for selected scars
  • Fractional CO₂ laser
  • PRP-supported procedures
  • Combination scar revision

Acne-scar procedures are available at both Aastha Skin Centre branches.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
Gentle cleansing

Cleanse without aggressive rubbing or frequent scrubbing.

Non-comedogenic moisturiser

Acne treatments can cause dryness. A suitable moisturiser may improve comfort and adherence.

Sunscreen

Sun protection helps reduce worsening of post-acne marks and supports the skin during treatment.

Prescribed acne treatment

Apply medicines in the amount and frequency advised by the dermatologist.

Suitable cosmetics

Choose products labelled non-comedogenic or less likely to block pores.

More products do not necessarily mean better acne control. Combining several strong ingredients without guidance can damage the skin barrier.

Does diet cause acne?

Diet is not the only cause of acne. Some people may notice that particular dietary patterns appear to influence their breakouts, but restrictive diets should not replace appropriate medical treatment.

Patients can maintain a balanced diet and observe whether a consistent personal trigger exists. NICE reviewed dietary evidence while developing its acne guideline, but acne care remains centred on evidence-based skin treatment tailored to the individual.

Can stress worsen acne?

Stress may worsen breakouts in some people through hormonal and behavioural pathways. Stress can also affect sleep, skincare consistency and picking behaviour.

Managing stress may support overall wellbeing, but stress reduction alone may not control moderate or severe acne.

Acne treatment during pregnancy

Acne treatment during pregnancy or while trying to conceive requires special care because several common acne medicines are not suitable.

Patients should tell the dermatologist when they:

  • Are pregnant
  • Are trying to conceive
  • Are breastfeeding
  • Have recently stopped contraception
  • Are taking hormonal treatment

Do not continue or start prescription acne medicine during pregnancy without guidance from a qualified medical professional.

Acne treatment for teenagers

Teenage acne should not automatically be dismissed as something that must simply be endured.

Early assessment may help:

  • Reduce painful inflammation
  • Prevent avoidable scars
  • Improve treatment habits
  • Reduce inappropriate home remedies
  • Support confidence and wellbeing

Parents and teenagers should understand that improvement usually requires consistent treatment over time.

Acne treatment for adults

Adult acne may differ from teenage acne in pattern, triggers and treatment considerations.

An adult-acne assessment may review:

  • Menstrual pattern
  • Hormonal symptoms
  • Pregnancy plans
  • Current cosmetics
  • Hair and skin products
  • Medicines
  • Stress and sleep
  • Previous acne treatment
  • Scarring tendency

Treatment is customised rather than based solely on age.

introduction: Dermatologist-led assessment and personalised care for alopecia areata, available at Karan Nagar and Paloura Chowk.

value.heading: What is alopecia areata?
value.body:
Alopecia areata is a chronic, unpredictable autoimmune hair-loss condition.

The immune system mistakenly targets hair follicles during their active growth phase. This causes affected hairs to shed, often leaving one or more smooth bald patches.

The follicles are generally not permanently destroyed, which means regrowth remains possible. However, the amount, speed and durability of regrowth differ greatly between patients.

value.heading: What are the common signs?
value.body:
Possible signs include:

  • One or more smooth round bald patches
  • Oval areas of sudden hair loss
  • Patchy beard loss
  • Eyebrow or eyelash loss
  • Short broken hairs near the patch border
  • Fine regrowing hairs
  • White or grey regrowth
  • Nail pitting or roughness
  • Tingling, itching or burning before hair falls

The scalp skin often looks normal rather than scaly, crusted or severely inflamed.

value.heading: What is patchy alopecia areata?
value.body:
Patchy alopecia areata is the most familiar form.

It produces one or several smooth areas of hair loss on the scalp, beard or body. A small number of recent patches may regrow spontaneously, particularly when the disease has been present for less than a year.

Treatment may still be considered when the patches are enlarging, visible, recurring or distressing.

value.heading: What is alopecia totalis?
value.body:
Alopecia totalis means near-complete or complete loss of scalp hair.

It represents a more extensive form of alopecia areata. Eyebrows, eyelashes or body hair may also be affected.

Spontaneous full regrowth is less predictable than it is in limited patchy disease, and systemic treatment assessment may be considered.

value.heading: What is alopecia universalis?
value.body:
Alopecia universalis causes extensive loss of hair from the scalp and body.

It may involve:

  • Scalp hair
  • Eyebrows
  • Eyelashes
  • Beard
  • Underarm hair
  • Pubic hair
  • Other body hair

The condition is not dangerous by itself, but loss of eyelashes, eyebrows and nostril hair reduces some natural protection from sunlight, dust and airborne particles.

value.heading: What is ophiasis-pattern alopecia?
value.body:
Ophiasis describes a band-like pattern of hair loss around the:

  • Back of the scalp
  • Sides of the scalp
  • Area above the ears

This pattern can be more resistant to treatment than one or two central scalp patches.

It should be distinguished from traction alopecia, fungal infection and other conditions affecting the scalp margins.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Is alopecia areata a scarring hair-loss condition?

Usually not.

Alopecia areata is classified as non-scarring alopecia. The skin within a typical patch usually remains smooth, and the follicular openings are preserved.

This distinction matters because scarring alopecias permanently damage hair follicles and may require rapid anti-inflammatory treatment to prevent irreversible loss.

A patch that is painful, inflamed, shiny, scarred or associated with pustules should be assessed for another diagnosis.

What are exclamation-mark hairs?

Exclamation-mark hairs are short hairs that become narrower near the scalp and wider towards the tip.

They may be seen around the edge of an active alopecia areata patch. They are not present in every patient, and their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.

A dermatologist may identify them using close examination or dermoscopy.

How does alopecia areata appear on Indian hair and skin?

The bald area usually appears smooth regardless of skin tone.

On Indian skin, the contrast between the scalp and dark hair can make even a small patch highly visible. Broken hairs, black dots and fine regrowth may be easier to appreciate with dermoscopy.

Temporary changes in scalp colour can also result from:

  • Sun exposure on a newly bare patch
  • Previous irritating treatments
  • Steroid misuse
  • Fungal infection
  • Scratching or inflammation

The diagnosis should not be based only on the shape of the patch.

Can alopecia areata affect the beard?

Yes.

Beard alopecia areata can produce one or more smooth hairless patches on the:

  • Chin
  • Jawline
  • Cheeks
  • Moustache area
  • Neck

It can resemble fungal beard infection, shaving irritation or scarring disease. Scaling, pus, pain or significant inflammation may indicate another cause.

Treatment options are selected according to patch size, duration and facial-skin sensitivity.

Can eyebrows and eyelashes be affected?

Yes.

Alopecia areata may cause partial or complete loss of eyebrows or eyelashes.

Eyelash loss can increase irritation from:

  • Dust
  • Wind
  • Sunlight
  • Dryness
  • Small particles entering the eyes

Glasses or sunglasses may provide practical protection. Artificial eyebrows, temporary cosmetics or carefully selected medical treatment may also be discussed.

Eye pain, marked redness or visual change requires appropriate eye assessment.

Can alopecia areata affect the nails?

Yes.

Possible nail changes include:

  • Tiny pits
  • Rough surface
  • Brittle nails
  • Longitudinal ridging
  • Thinning
  • Splitting
  • Crumbling in severe cases

Nail changes can occur with limited or extensive hair loss. Patients should mention them because they may help support the diagnosis and assess disease burden.

Is alopecia areata contagious?

No.

Alopecia areata cannot spread through:

  • Touching
  • Sharing combs
  • Towels
  • Pillows
  • Haircuts
  • Food
  • Swimming
  • Living together

It is an immune-mediated condition, not a fungal, bacterial or viral infection.

Is alopecia areata caused by poor hair care?

No.

It is not caused by:

  • Dirty hair
  • Infrequent shampooing
  • Dandruff alone
  • Applying oil
  • Cutting the hair too short
  • Sharing a comb
  • Eating a particular food
  • Failure to take supplements

Hair products or tight hairstyles can cause other types of hair loss, but they do not explain ordinary autoimmune alopecia areata.

What causes alopecia areata?

The exact trigger cannot always be identified.

The condition appears to involve:

  • Autoimmune activity
  • Genetic susceptibility
  • Immune signalling around hair follicles
  • Environmental influences
  • Possible illness or stress-related triggers in some patients

A relative may have alopecia areata or another autoimmune condition, but many patients have no affected family member.

Does stress cause alopecia areata?

Stress may precede or aggravate hair loss in some people, but it is not the sole explanation for the disease.

Alopecia areata involves measurable immune activity around hair follicles. Telling a patient to “stop stressing” is neither a diagnosis nor a complete treatment plan.

Stress management can support wellbeing, especially when visible hair loss causes anxiety, but it does not replace dermatological care.

Can children develop alopecia areata?

Yes.

Alopecia areata can begin during childhood and may cause:

  • One or more scalp patches
  • Eyebrow or eyelash loss
  • Nail pitting
  • Recurrent episodes
  • Distress at school
  • Bullying or unwanted attention

Some children with limited disease regrow hair without treatment. When treatment is needed, age, disease extent, discomfort and treatment burden must be considered. Topical corticosteroids are commonly considered before painful scalp injections in young children.

Is alopecia areata associated with other conditions?

People with alopecia areata have a higher likelihood of certain immune-related conditions, including:

  • Autoimmune thyroid disease
  • Atopic dermatitis or eczema
  • Vitiligo
  • Other autoimmune disorders in selected patients

This does not mean every patient needs a large panel of blood tests or will develop another disease. Investigation should be guided by symptoms, history and examination.

Which symptoms should be mentioned during consultation?

Tell Dr. Cheena Langer about:

  • Unexplained tiredness
  • Weight change
  • Heat or cold intolerance
  • Palpitations
  • White skin patches
  • Persistent eczema
  • Joint symptoms
  • Other autoimmune disease
  • New medicine use
  • Recent illness
  • Family history of hair loss or autoimmunity

These details may influence the investigation and treatment plan.

Is every round bald patch alopecia areata?

No.

Other possible causes include:

  • Scalp ringworm
  • Hair pulling
  • Traction alopecia
  • Pattern hair loss
  • Telogen effluvium
  • Scarring alopecia
  • Lupus-related hair loss
  • Syphilitic alopecia
  • Pressure or friction
  • Hair-shaft breakage

Treatment differs significantly between these conditions, so diagnosis should come before steroid injections, minoxidil, antifungal tablets or hair procedures.

How is alopecia areata different from scalp ringworm?

  • Smooth bald patches
  • Normal-looking scalp
  • Exclamation-mark hairs
  • Nail changes
  • No contagious infection
  • Scaling
  • Broken hairs
  • Black dots
  • Itching
  • Tender swelling
  • Pus
  • Enlarged neck lymph nodes
  • Infection in children or household contacts

Scalp ringworm generally requires prescription oral antifungal medicine. Steroid treatment without antifungal therapy can worsen or mask infection.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
How is it different from pattern hair loss?

  • Widening of the central parting
  • Reduced crown density
  • Receding temples
  • Gradual miniaturisation
  • Family history
  • Sudden round patches
  • Beard, eyebrow or eyelash involvement
  • Nail changes
  • Unpredictable regrowth and relapse

A person can have both conditions at the same time.

How does Dr. Cheena Langer diagnose alopecia areata?

A consultation may include:

  • Reviewing how suddenly the loss began
  • Examining the scalp and other hair-bearing areas
  • Checking eyebrows, eyelashes and beard
  • Examining fingernails and toenails
  • Looking for scale, inflammation or scarring
  • Using dermoscopy for a magnified view
  • Reviewing medicines and recent illness
  • Asking about family and autoimmune history
  • Assessing emotional and social impact
  • Considering blood tests or scalp biopsy

Alopecia areata can often be diagnosed from history, examination and dermoscopy.

What is scalp dermoscopy?

Dermoscopy uses a handheld magnifying instrument to examine the scalp and hair more closely.

It may reveal features such as:

  • Yellow dots
  • Black dots
  • Broken hairs
  • Tapering hairs
  • Short regrowing hairs
  • Preserved follicular openings

Dermoscopy can help distinguish alopecia areata from fungal infection, hair pulling, pattern loss and scarring alopecia.

Are blood tests always required?

No.

Blood tests may be considered when:

  • Thyroid symptoms are present
  • Hair loss is diffuse rather than clearly patchy
  • Iron deficiency is possible
  • Diet or nutritional history raises concern
  • Another autoimmune disease is suspected
  • Systemic treatment is being planned

The diagnosis remains uncertain

Possible testing may include thyroid, blood-count, iron or selected vitamin assessment. Testing should be individualised rather than ordered as an automatic large “hair-loss package.”

When might a scalp biopsy be needed?

A scalp biopsy may be recommended when:

  • The diagnosis remains uncertain
  • The scalp looks inflamed or scarred
  • Treatment has not produced the expected response
  • Lupus or another scarring alopecia is suspected
  • Hair pulling and alopecia areata remain difficult to distinguish
  • Several forms of hair loss may be present together

A small sample is removed under local anaesthesia and examined microscopically.

Will the hair grow back?

Regrowth is possible, especially when there are only one or two recent patches.

Hair may initially regrow as:

  • Fine colourless hair
  • White or grey hair
  • Short soft hair
  • Hair that gradually thickens and regains colour

Some patients experience complete regrowth, while others have partial regrowth, recurrence or progression. The course is unpredictable.

Can alopecia areata return after regrowth?

Yes.

Hair may regrow and later fall again in the same or another area. Relapse does not necessarily mean the earlier treatment was performed incorrectly.

The condition can follow several patterns:

  • One isolated episode
  • Repeated limited patches
  • Long stable intervals
  • Gradual extension
  • Extensive scalp or body involvement

Long-term follow-up may be useful when episodes recur.

Which factors can make regrowth less predictable?

A more difficult course may be associated with:

  • Extensive scalp involvement
  • Alopecia totalis or universalis
  • Ophiasis pattern
  • Long disease duration
  • Repeated relapse
  • Nail involvement
  • Early childhood onset
  • Loss of eyebrows and eyelashes
  • Other autoimmune conditions
  • White hair within affected patches

These are general prognostic factors, not guarantees of a poor result. Treatment decisions should remain individualised.

Hair-loss diagnosis before procedures

Alopecia areata is distinguished from fungal infection, hair pulling, pattern hair loss, traction and scarring alopecia.

Scalp, beard, eyebrows, eyelashes and nails examined

The consultation assesses disease beyond the most visible scalp patch.

Dermatologist-led management

Care is planned under Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist.

Treatment matched to disease extent

Observation, local medicine, injection assessment and systemic-treatment evaluation are considered according to age and severity.

Focused testing

Blood tests or biopsy are selected when they may change diagnosis or treatment—not ordered automatically for every patient.

Realistic expectations

The clinic does not promise permanent cure, complete regrowth or identical responses in every patient.

Need help choosing?

Sudden bald patches should be diagnosed before using antifungal creams, supplements or hair procedures

items.question: Can alopecia areata be cured permanently?
items.answer: There is currently no guaranteed permanent cure. Treatment can encourage regrowth and control disease activity, but hair loss may recur.

items.question: Does every patient need treatment?
items.answer:
No.

Observation may be reasonable when:

  • Only one or two small patches are present
  • Hair loss has been present for less than a year
  • Regrowth is already visible
  • The patient prefers not to use medicine
  • Treatment burden exceeds the expected benefit

Many people with mild disease regrow hair without treatment. The decision also depends on visibility, emotional impact, age and the patient’s preferences.

items.question: What are the goals of treatment?
items.answer:
Treatment may aim to:

  • Stop enlargement of existing patches
  • Reduce the appearance of new patches
  • Stimulate scalp-hair regrowth
  • Support eyebrow or eyelash recovery
  • Maintain newly grown hair
  • Treat nail involvement
  • Reduce distress
  • Protect exposed scalp and eyes

The goal is not always complete regrowth. Partial improvement or disease stabilisation may still be meaningful.

items.question: Are corticosteroid injections used?
items.answer:
Small injections of corticosteroid into bald patches are commonly considered for limited patchy alopecia areata in adults.

Treatment may be repeated at intervals when appropriate. Possible side effects include:

  • Injection discomfort
  • Temporary dents or thinning in the skin
  • Visible small blood vessels
  • Colour change
  • Incomplete regrowth
  • Recurrence

AAD guidance describes intralesional corticosteroids as an established option for adults with a few patches.

Current procedure availability, branch and appointment requirements should be confirmed before booking.

items.question: Are topical steroid medicines used?
items.answer:
Yes.

A prescription corticosteroid applied to the patch may be considered for:

  • Children
  • Patients who prefer to avoid injections
  • Sensitive areas
  • Several limited patches
  • Selected active margins

The correct potency, formulation and duration depend on age and body area.

Prolonged unsupervised use can cause skin thinning, visible vessels, folliculitis or colour changes.

items.question: Does minoxidil treat alopecia areata?
items.answer:
Minoxidil may support or maintain regrowth in selected patients, but it does not directly correct the autoimmune process causing alopecia areata.

It is often used as an adjunct after regrowth begins rather than as the only treatment for actively spreading disease.

Possible effects include:

  • Scalp irritation
  • Unwanted facial hair
  • Initial temporary shedding
  • Need for continued use
  • Loss of supported regrowth after stopping

It should be used only after confirming the diagnosis and suitable strength.

items.question: What is anthralin treatment?
items.answer:
Anthralin is an older topical medicine that deliberately creates controlled irritation around the affected follicles.

It may be considered in selected patients, particularly when other topical approaches are unsuitable.

Possible effects include:

  • Redness
  • Irritation
  • Burning
  • Temporary staining of skin
  • Staining of clothing or surfaces

Application time and frequency must be prescribed carefully.

value.heading: What does “black neck” mean?
value.body:
“Black neck” is a patient-friendly description rather than one specific diagnosis.

Darkening around the neck can result from:

  • Acanthosis nigricans
  • Friction
  • Post-inflammatory pigmentation
  • Contact dermatitis
  • Repeated rubbing or scrubbing
  • A fungal or bacterial condition
  • Product irritation
  • A medicine reaction
  • Another pigment disorder

The cause should be identified before using bleaching creams, scrubs, peels or home remedies.

value.heading: What is acanthosis nigricans?
value.body:
Acanthosis nigricans is a skin condition that causes one or more areas to become:

  • Darker
  • Thicker
  • Velvety
  • Slightly raised
  • More textured than nearby skin

It usually develops gradually in body folds. Although the affected skin is often harmless, the change may be a visible sign of an underlying metabolic or hormonal condition.

value.heading: What is the most common cause?
value.body:
Excess body weight and associated insulin resistance are among the most common causes of acanthosis nigricans in adults and children.

However, the condition can also occur in:

  • People with a healthy body weight
  • People with a family history
  • Patients taking certain medicines
  • People with hormonal conditions
  • Patients with another medical disorder

A person should not be diagnosed solely from body size.

value.heading: What is insulin resistance?
value.body:
Insulin is a hormone that helps glucose move from the blood into cells.

Insulin resistance means that the body’s cells do not respond to insulin as effectively as expected. The body may then produce more insulin to maintain normal blood glucose. High insulin levels can stimulate skin growth pathways and contribute to acanthosis nigricans.

A person can have insulin resistance before routine blood glucose reaches the diabetes range.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Is black neck caused by dirt?

Usually not.

Acanthosis nigricans cannot be washed or scrubbed away because the darker appearance comes from changes within the skin rather than surface dirt. Vigorous scrubbing can irritate the area and make the colour or texture more noticeable.

Patients and children should not be blamed for being “unclean.”

Is acanthosis nigricans contagious?

No.

It cannot spread through:

  • Touching
  • Towels
  • Clothing
  • Sharing a bed
  • Swimming
  • Kissing
  • Sexual contact
  • Living in the same household

Acanthosis nigricans is not a bacterial, viral or contagious fungal infection.

What does acanthosis nigricans look and feel like?

Typical features include:

  • Brown, grey-brown or darkened skin
  • Thickened texture
  • A soft, velvety surface
  • Increased skin lines
  • Small raised projections
  • Skin tags
  • Occasional itching
  • Odour in moist skin folds

The change often develops slowly over months or years.

Where does acanthosis nigricans appear?

Common sites include:

  • Back and sides of the neck
  • Underarms
  • Groin
  • Inner thighs
  • Beneath the breasts
  • Elbows
  • Knees
  • Knuckles
  • Around the navel

Less commonly, it may affect the face, eyelids, lips, palms, soles, nipples or genital region.

Can acanthosis nigricans cause skin tags?

Yes.

Small skin tags may develop within or around the thickened area, especially on the neck or underarms. Both conditions can be associated with friction and metabolic factors, although skin tags can also occur in otherwise healthy people.

Skin-tag removal may improve the individual growths but does not treat the underlying cause of acanthosis nigricans.

How does black neck appear on Indian skin?

Acanthosis nigricans can be particularly visible on Indian and other brown skin tones.

The affected area may appear:

  • Light brown
  • Dark brown
  • Grey-brown
  • Nearly black
  • Unevenly coloured
  • More textured than surrounding skin

The condition is more commonly recognised in people with brown or black skin, but it can affect any skin tone.

Does black neck mean someone has diabetes?

Not always.

Acanthosis nigricans can be associated with:

  • Insulin resistance
  • Prediabetes
  • Type 2 diabetes
  • Obesity
  • PCOS
  • Thyroid or adrenal conditions
  • Medicines
  • Familial tendency

It is a reason to consider metabolic assessment, not proof that diabetes is already present.

Can black neck be an early sign of prediabetes?

Yes.

A dark, velvety band around the neck or another body fold can be one of the visible signs associated with prediabetes or insulin resistance. Testing and appropriate lifestyle changes may identify metabolic risk before type 2 diabetes becomes established.

The skin sign should be assessed alongside medical history, examination and laboratory results.

Is acanthosis nigricans associated with PCOS?

Yes. Polycystic ovary syndrome, commonly called PCOS, can be associated with insulin resistance and acanthosis nigricans.

Other possible PCOS-related symptoms include:

  • Irregular periods
  • Acne
  • Excess facial or body hair
  • Scalp-hair thinning
  • Difficulty managing weight
  • Fertility concerns

Patients with this combination may require coordinated dermatology, gynaecology or medical assessment.

Can children and teenagers develop black neck?

Yes.

Acanthosis nigricans can occur in children and adolescents and may be associated with:

  • Insulin resistance
  • Family history of diabetes
  • Increased body weight
  • Puberty-related hormonal change
  • PCOS in adolescent girls
  • Certain medicines
  • Familial acanthosis nigricans

The child should not be shamed, scrubbed aggressively or placed on an extreme diet. Medical assessment and age-appropriate family support are more useful.

Can a thin or normal-weight person have acanthosis nigricans?

Yes.

Possible explanations include:

  • A genetic or familial form
  • Hormonal disease
  • A medicine
  • Early insulin resistance
  • Another skin diagnosis
  • A rare underlying illness

No identifiable medical cause

Testing should be based on the patient’s complete history rather than assuming that acanthosis nigricans only affects people who are overweight.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
Which medicines may cause acanthosis nigricans?

Reported medicine-related associations include:

  • Systemic corticosteroids
  • Some hormone treatments
  • Oral contraceptive pills
  • High-dose niacin
  • Selected medicines that influence insulin or hormone pathways

Patients should not stop a prescribed medicine independently. Dr. Cheena Langer may review the timeline and coordinate with the prescribing doctor when a medicine-related cause is possible.

Can acanthosis nigricans be inherited?

Yes.

Familial or genetic acanthosis nigricans can occur in otherwise healthy people and may affect several members of the same family. It may begin during childhood or puberty and is not necessarily associated with diabetes.

A family history should still be considered alongside metabolic risk.

Can black neck rarely be associated with cancer?

Rarely, sudden and extensive acanthosis nigricans can be associated with an internal malignancy.

Features that need prompt medical assessment include:

  • Rapid onset
  • Widespread thickening
  • Severe itching
  • Mouth or lip involvement
  • Palms becoming unusually thick
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • New disease in an older adult

No obvious metabolic explanation

This presentation is uncommon. Most patients with gradual neck or underarm acanthosis nigricans do not have cancer.

Diagnosis before cosmetic treatment

The neck is assessed for acanthosis nigricans, friction, contact dermatitis, fungal infection and other causes of pigmentation.

Metabolic and hormonal clues considered

The consultation includes relevant history of diabetes, PCOS, periods, medicines and family risk.

Treatment suitable for Indian skin

Irritation and post-inflammatory pigmentation risks are considered before selecting active creams, peels or procedures.

Realistic expectations

The clinic does not promise instant clearing or claim that a cosmetic procedure can cure insulin resistance.

Need help choosing?

A dark neck may be more than a cosmetic concern—get the cause assessed before scrubbing or bleaching it

  • Cause of the pigmentation
  • Prescription cream or moisturiser
  • Blood-glucose or hormone tests
  • PCOS or medical referral
  • Skin biopsy in an uncertain case
  • Chemical-peel suitability
  • Laser or another procedure
  • Number of treatment sessions
  • Follow-up after the included 10-day period

A cosmetic procedure may not be needed when treating the underlying medical factor and using an appropriate topical plan produces satisfactory improvement.

value.heading: How care is planned
value.body:
• Assessment comes before treatment selection.
  • Options, limitations, aftercare and expected timelines are explained.

items.question: When should black neck be assessed promptly?
items.answer:
Arrange timely medical review when:

  • Darkening develops suddenly
  • The affected area spreads rapidly
  • The mouth or lips are involved
  • The palms or soles become thick
  • There is unexplained weight loss
  • The patient feels generally unwell
  • Severe itching begins
  • A child develops significant metabolic symptoms
  • The appearance does not fit ordinary gradual acanthosis nigricans

Sudden widespread disease should not be managed only with a cosmetic cream.

items.question: Is every dark neck acanthosis nigricans?
items.answer:
No.

Conditions that may resemble it include:

  • Frictional pigmentation
  • Post-inflammatory pigmentation
  • Contact dermatitis
  • Terra firma-forme dermatosis
  • Dermatosis neglecta
  • Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis
  • Lichen planus pigmentosus
  • Fungal infection
  • Drug-related pigmentation
  • Addison disease
  • Normal variation in skin colour

The texture, distribution, symptoms, product history and associated health findings help distinguish these conditions.

items.question: Can fungal infection cause a dark neck?
items.answer:
A fungal condition can sometimes produce darker or lighter patches, itching or fine scale, but it usually does not produce the classic thick, velvety texture of acanthosis nigricans.

Antifungal treatment should not be continued for months without confirming that fungus is present.

items.question: Can jewellery, perfume or hair products darken the neck?
items.answer:
Yes.

Contact dermatitis caused by perfume, hair dye, shampoo, jewellery or skincare can produce:

  • Itching
  • Burning
  • Scaling
  • Inflammation
  • Dark post-inflammatory marks

This pattern often differs from the symmetrical velvety thickening of acanthosis nigricans.

items.question: How does Dr. Cheena Langer diagnose black neck?
items.answer:
A consultation may include:

  • Examining the neck and other body folds
  • Assessing whether the skin feels velvety or thick
  • Checking for skin tags
  • Reviewing when the change began
  • Asking about weight, periods and hormonal symptoms
  • Reviewing family history of diabetes
  • Checking medicines and supplements
  • Looking for fungal infection or dermatitis
  • Assessing signs of insulin resistance
  • Considering blood tests or referral

Acanthosis nigricans is usually recognised through clinical examination, while tests help determine whether an underlying condition is contributing.

items.question: Which tests may be considered?
items.answer:
Depending on the patient’s age, symptoms and medical history, assessment may include:

  • Fasting blood glucose
  • HbA1c
  • Lipid profile
  • Liver-function assessment
  • Thyroid tests
  • Blood pressure
  • Waist and body-weight assessment
  • PCOS-related evaluation
  • Other hormone tests when indicated

Not every patient needs every test. The investigation plan should be targeted rather than sold as a standard “black neck package.”

items.question: Is a skin biopsy required?
items.answer:
Usually not.

A biopsy may be considered when:

  • The appearance is unusual
  • Another pigment disorder is suspected
  • Disease develops rapidly
  • The diagnosis remains uncertain
  • Treatment repeatedly fails
  • A rare cause needs exclusion

Skin biopsy is confirmed as available at both Aastha Skin Centre branches when clinically required.

value.body:
