value.heading: What is a hair transplant?
value.body:
A hair transplant is a surgical hair-restoration procedure in which naturally growing hair follicles are moved from one part of the scalp to another.

The procedure does not create unlimited new follicles. It redistributes a limited supply of existing donor hair to improve coverage in selected thinning or bald areas.

Modern procedures commonly use small follicular-unit grafts containing one or several hairs. These grafts are positioned to recreate appropriate direction, angle and density.

value.heading: Which type of hair loss is commonly treated?
value.body:
Hair transplantation is most commonly considered for androgenetic alopecia, also called:

  • Male-pattern hair loss
  • Female-pattern hair loss
  • Hereditary patterned hair thinning

It may also be considered for selected stable cases involving:

  • Receding frontal hairline
  • Temporal recession
  • Crown thinning
  • Hairline correction
  • Stable traction alopecia
  • Selected surgical or traumatic scars
  • Carefully selected inactive scarring alopecia

Not every form of hair loss is suitable for transplantation. Diagnosis should come before surgical planning.

value.heading: Why is hair-loss diagnosis necessary first?
value.body:
Hair can shed or thin because of many different conditions, including:

  • Pattern hair loss
  • Thyroid or nutritional problems
  • Recent illness
  • Stress-related shedding
  • Alopecia areata
  • Fungal scalp infection
  • Traction alopecia
  • Scarring alopecia
  • Medication effects
  • Post-pregnancy shedding

A transplant does not treat the underlying cause of active, temporary or inflammatory hair loss. A dermatologist may use scalp examination, dermoscopy, blood tests or scalp biopsy to identify the diagnosis before surgery is considered.

value.heading: Who may be suitable for a hair transplant?
value.body:
A potentially suitable candidate generally needs:

  • A confirmed type of permanent hair loss
  • Adequate healthy donor hair
  • Reasonably stable hair-loss progression
  • A healthy scalp
  • Realistic density expectations
  • Sufficient healing capacity
  • Willingness to follow aftercare
  • Understanding that native hair may continue thinning

The AAD identifies adequate donor hair and the ability to grow hair in the recipient area as two essential requirements.

value.heading: Who may need to postpone the procedure?
value.body:
A hair transplant may be postponed when there is:

  • Rapidly progressing hair loss
  • Severe active dandruff or dermatitis
  • Scalp infection
  • Active alopecia areata
  • Active scarring alopecia
  • Inflamed or painful scalp disease
  • Poorly controlled diabetes
  • Significant bleeding risk
  • Unrealistic expectations
  • Inadequate donor density
  • A very young patient with an unpredictable future pattern

Treating an unstable scalp condition first may reduce the risk of graft loss, poor healing or an unnatural result as hair loss progresses.

value.heading: What is the donor area?
value.body:
The donor area is the part of the scalp from which follicles are harvested.

It usually includes selected areas at the back and sides of the head because these follicles are often more resistant to the hormonal influence involved in pattern hair loss. The size and quality of the donor supply limit how much coverage can realistically be created.

Assessment may include:

  • Donor density
  • Hair-shaft thickness
  • Number of hairs per follicular unit
  • Hair curl and colour
  • Scalp flexibility
  • Existing scars
  • Miniaturisation within the donor zone
  • Previous transplant harvesting

The donor area is finite and must be preserved for present and possible future needs.

value.heading: What is follicular unit excision or FUE?
value.body:
Follicular unit excision, commonly called FUE, removes follicular units individually using small circular punches.

The grafts are then prepared and placed into recipient sites in the thinning area. FUE leaves numerous small punctate scars rather than one long linear scar.

Possible advantages include:

  • No long strip scar
  • Greater flexibility with shorter hairstyles
  • Individual graft harvesting
  • Usually less tension at the donor wound

Limitations can include:

  • Need to trim or shave donor hair in many cases
  • Longer harvesting time
  • Visible dot scars with very short shaving
  • Risk of overharvesting
  • Risk of graft transection
  • Limited donor supply

FUE should not be advertised as completely scarless.

value.heading: What is follicular unit transplantation or FUT?
value.body:
Follicular unit transplantation, or FUT, involves removing a narrow strip of hair-bearing scalp from the donor area.

The strip is divided into individual follicular-unit grafts, and the donor wound is closed with stitches. FUT generally leaves a linear scar that may be concealed by surrounding hair.

FUT may be considered when:

  • A relatively large number of grafts is required
  • Donor preservation is a priority
  • The patient normally keeps longer hair
  • Scalp flexibility is suitable
  • A linear scar is acceptable

The exact technique available through Aastha Skin Centre must be confirmed before it is advertised as a clinic-specific service.

value.heading: Is FUE better than FUT?
value.body:
Neither technique is automatically superior for every patient.

Research reviews find that both FUE and FUT can produce high-quality follicular-unit grafts. Their main differences involve donor harvesting, scar pattern, recovery, graft numbers and suitability for future procedures.

FUE may be preferred when

  • The patient wants to avoid a long linear scar
  • Short hairstyles are important
  • Scalp tightness limits strip removal
  • Only a selected graft number is needed

FUT may be considered when

  • A larger graft harvest is planned
  • Donor density must be managed conservatively
  • The patient can conceal a linear scar
  • Repeat surgical planning favours strip harvesting

The choice should follow scalp assessment and long-term donor planning.

value.heading: What is DHI hair transplant?
value.body:
DHI, or direct hair implantation, is commonly used as a marketing term for graft placement with an implanter device.

In many cases, the follicles are still harvested using an FUE-type method. An implanter pen changes how grafts are placed; it does not automatically create a completely separate biological form of hair transplantation. Implanter tools are among several accepted graft-placement methods described in surgical literature.

DHI should not automatically be described as:

  • Scar-free
  • Painless
  • More successful than every other method
  • A guarantee of higher density
  • Suitable for every patient

Aastha Skin Centre should only advertise DHI when the exact technique, equipment and operating-team training have been verified.

value.heading: How is a natural-looking hairline planned?
value.body:
Hairline design affects the long-term appearance of the transplant.

Planning considers:

  • Age
  • Facial proportions
  • Existing frontal hair
  • Future hair-loss pattern
  • Donor supply
  • Hair calibre
  • Direction and angle of growth
  • Temporal recession
  • Desired hairstyle

A conservative hairline may remain more natural as the patient ages and help preserve donor grafts for future thinning. Fine single-hair grafts are commonly used near the front, with larger follicular units placed farther behind for density.

An unusually low or perfectly straight hairline can appear artificial and consume excessive donor hair.

value.heading: How is the number of grafts estimated?
value.body:
The estimated graft number depends on:

  • Size of the thinning area
  • Existing hair density
  • Degree of baldness
  • Donor density
  • Hair-shaft thickness
  • Hair-to-skin colour contrast
  • Curl or wave
  • Previous transplant surgery
  • Desired coverage
  • Need to reserve donor hair

A graft is not always the same as a single hair. One follicular-unit graft may contain one, two, three or more hair shafts.

An exact graft number cannot be promised from a photograph alone. Physical scalp examination is usually needed.

value.heading: What happens during a hair transplant?
value.body:
A typical procedure may involve:

  • Confirming the surgical plan
  • Photographing and marking the scalp
  • Designing the hairline
  • Trimming or shaving selected hair
  • Cleaning the scalp
  • Administering local anaesthetic
  • Harvesting donor follicular units
  • Preparing and storing the grafts
  • Creating recipient sites
  • Placing grafts at planned angles and directions
  • Dressing or cleaning the donor area
  • Providing postoperative instructions

Hair-transplant surgery frequently takes several hours, and a large session may continue over more than one day. Most patients remain awake under local anaesthesia.

Diagnosis before surgery

The cause and stability of hair loss are assessed before transplantation is recommended.

Donor-area planning

Donor density, miniaturisation, hair calibre and future requirements are considered before estimating graft availability.

Dermatologist-led evaluation

Assessment is provided under Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist.

Medical and surgical planning

Patients can be advised about medicines, PRP/GFC, transplantation and non-surgical alternatives according to diagnosis.

Realistic expectations

The goal is improved coverage—not unlimited grafts, guaranteed density or completely scar-free surgery.

Need help choosing?

A successful transplant begins with the correct hair-loss diagnosis and a realistic donor plan

items.question: Is a hair transplant painful?
items.answer:
Local-anaesthetic injections may briefly sting or burn.

Once the scalp is numb, the patient may feel:

  • Pressure
  • Pulling
  • Movement
  • Vibration
  • Mild discomfort from remaining in one position

Temporary soreness, tightness or sensitivity may develop after the anaesthetic wears off. The procedure should not be described as completely painless.

items.question: Is a hair transplant permanent?
items.answer: Transplanted donor hair is intended to provide long-lasting growth, but surrounding native hair can continue thinning. Medical treatment and long-term planning may therefore remain necessary.

items.question: Why does transplanted hair fall out after surgery?
items.answer:
Many transplanted hair shafts shed during the first few weeks. This is usually an expected part of the growth cycle and does not necessarily mean the follicles have failed.

The AAD notes that transplanted hair commonly sheds between approximately two and eight weeks after surgery. The area may temporarily appear thinner before new growth becomes visible.

Patients should not judge the final result during this early shedding stage.

items.question: When does new hair growth begin?
items.answer:
The timeline varies, but patients may generally expect:

  • First two weeks: healing, redness and crusting
  • Two to eight weeks: shedding of transplanted shafts
  • Around three to four months: early new growth may begin
  • Six to nine months: more visible improvement
  • Around 12 months or later: fuller maturation in many patients

The AAD reports that many patients see noticeable results between six and nine months, while some require around 12 months. NHS guidance notes that full maturation can take longer in some cases.

Crown growth may mature more slowly than frontal hairline growth.

items.question: How long is recovery?
items.answer:
Recovery depends on the harvesting method, graft number and individual healing.

Common early effects include:

  • Swelling
  • Tightness
  • Tenderness
  • Redness
  • Small crusts
  • Temporary numbness
  • Donor-area discomfort
  • Mild itching

Patients must be especially careful during the first two weeks because the newly placed grafts are still healing. Time away from work may range from several days to around two weeks depending on the procedure and how visible the recovery is.

items.question: What is shock loss?
items.answer:
Shock loss means temporary shedding of transplanted or nearby existing hair after surgery.

It can occur because follicles enter a resting phase following surgical stress. In many cases, the affected hair regrows, but permanent loss may occur when nearby native follicles were already severely miniaturised.

Temporary effluvium or shock loss is a recognised hair-transplant complication and should be discussed before surgery.

items.question: What risks can occur?
items.answer:
Possible risks and complications include:

  • Pain
  • Swelling
  • Bleeding
  • Infection
  • Folliculitis
  • Crusting
  • Prolonged redness
  • Temporary numbness
  • Shock loss
  • Poor graft growth
  • Visible scarring
  • Donor overharvesting
  • Uneven density
  • Unnatural direction
  • An unnatural hairline
  • Small cysts
  • Pigmentation changes
  • Rare tissue necrosis

Recent reviews identify donor depletion, hypopigmented dot scars, folliculitis, prolonged redness, shock loss and recipient-site injury among recognised FUE-related complications.

introduction: Understand how focused ultrasound and radiofrequency differ, and which approach may suit your skin, goals and acceptable downtime.

value.heading: Two technologies, different treatment depths
value.body:
HIFU and radiofrequency are non-surgical energy-based treatments used for selected concerns related to skin laxity. They are not interchangeable and neither is a substitute for surgery when laxity is marked.

A consultation is needed to assess skin quality, facial volume, treatment area, medical history and realistic goals before choosing a procedure.

value.heading: How HIFU works
value.body:
High-intensity focused ultrasound delivers energy at selected depths beneath the skin. It may be considered for suitable patients seeking gradual improvement in mild to moderate laxity, particularly around the lower face, jawline or neck.

Results develop gradually and vary between patients. Treatment parameters and suitability depend on anatomy, tissue thickness and the device being used.

Read the detailed HIFU guide

value.heading: How radiofrequency works
value.body:
Radiofrequency uses controlled heat within targeted tissue. Different RF devices deliver energy in different ways; some are applied at the surface while others use insulated or non-insulated microneedles.

The expected effect, recovery and treatment schedule therefore depend on the specific technology, settings and indication rather than the label “RF” alone.

Read the detailed RF skin-tightening guide

value.heading: HIFU and RF at a glance
value.body:
• HIFU: focused ultrasound delivered at selected deeper tissue planes
  • RF: controlled radiofrequency heating, with depth depending on the device
  • Best choice: determined by examination, not by age alone
  • Results: gradual and variable; maintenance may be discussed
  • Downtime: depends on the method and individual response
  • Limitations: neither guarantees a surgical-lift result

value.heading: Who may need extra caution?
value.body: Tell the dermatologist about pregnancy, implanted electrical or metal devices, recent procedures, active infection, open wounds, altered sensation, medicines and any tendency to scar abnormally. Treatment may be postponed or avoided when safety or expected benefit is uncertain.

value.heading: Planning treatment
value.body:
• Assessment of laxity, skin quality and facial volume
  • Discussion of the area that concerns you
  • Review of previous procedures and medical history
  • Explanation of likely benefit and limitations
  • Choice of technology and treatment settings
  • Aftercare and review plan

More treatment is not always better. Excessive or unsuitable energy can cause unwanted effects, so conservative, anatomy-aware planning matters.

value.heading: How care is planned
value.body:
• Assessment comes before treatment selection.
  • Options, limitations, aftercare and expected timelines are explained.
  • The plan is adapted to diagnosis, skin type and medical history.

items.question: Which is better, HIFU or RF?
items.answer: Neither is universally better. The choice depends on the treatment depth required, skin quality, anatomy, goals and the exact device available.

items.question: Are the results immediate?
items.answer: Some patients notice an early change, but improvement is generally gradual and varies. Your dermatologist can explain the expected timeline for the selected method.

items.question: Can these treatments replace a facelift?
items.answer: No. Non-surgical energy treatments may offer modest improvement for selected patients but cannot reproduce the degree of correction possible with surgery.

items.question: How many sessions will I need?
items.answer: The number depends on the technology, indication and response. A session plan should be made only after assessment.

items.question: Is there downtime?
items.answer: Temporary redness, tenderness or swelling can occur. Downtime differs between surface RF, microneedling RF and focused ultrasound procedures.

items.question: Can HIFU and RF be combined?
items.answer: Combination treatment may be considered for selected patients, but it is not automatically necessary and should be planned around anatomy, timing and safety.

value.heading: What is HIFU?
value.body:
HIFU stands for high-intensity focused ultrasound.

Aesthetic focused-ultrasound devices deliver energy beneath the skin to create controlled heating in selected tissue layers. This controlled response may support tissue contraction and gradual collagen remodelling. The FDA classifies focused-ultrasound systems for aesthetic use as devices intended to produce temporary changes in physical appearance through localised tissue effects.

The results vary between devices, treatment protocols and patients. Evidence from one HIFU or microfocused-ultrasound platform should not automatically be applied to every machine.

value.heading: How does HIFU work?
value.body:
The treatment applicator directs ultrasound energy to planned depths beneath the skin. Energy is concentrated within small target zones, creating controlled heating while aiming to minimise unnecessary exposure to surrounding tissue.

The tissue response may involve:

  • Immediate contraction within treated tissue
  • A healing response
  • Gradual collagen remodelling
  • Progressive improvement in firmness

The FDA identifies thermal injury, mechanical injury, ocular injury and use error among the risks that manufacturers and operators must address for focused-ultrasound systems.

value.heading: How does Dr. Cheena Langer assess patients before HIFU?
value.body:
A consultation may include:

  • Examining the face and neck at rest and during movement
  • Assessing the degree of skin laxity
  • Distinguishing loose skin from facial-volume loss
  • Reviewing skin thickness and facial-fat distribution
  • Checking for acne, dermatitis, wounds or infection
  • Reviewing previous fillers, threads or energy treatments
  • Checking medicines and medical conditions
  • Reviewing implanted devices or metallic implants
  • Discussing the expected degree of improvement
  • Comparing HIFU with RF, fillers or surgical assessment

The treatment should be selected according to the patient’s concern and anatomy—not merely because HIFU is popular online.

value.heading: What happens during HIFU treatment?
value.body:
A typical appointment may involve:

  • Confirming and photographing the treatment area
  • Cleansing the skin
  • Marking anatomical boundaries
  • Applying ultrasound gel
  • Selecting suitable treatment depths and settings
  • Delivering focused-ultrasound pulses
  • Monitoring patient comfort
  • Checking the tissue response
  • Cleaning the treated area
  • Providing aftercare instructions

Complete contact between the applicator and skin is important. FDA guidance warns that inadequate contact can contribute to unintended exposure and injury.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
What concerns may HIFU address?

After clinical assessment, HIFU may be considered for selected concerns such as:

  • Mild lower-face laxity
  • Early jowling
  • Reduced jawline definition
  • Loose skin beneath the chin
  • Mild neck laxity
  • Selected brow or facial-lifting concerns
  • Gradual age-related loss of firmness

Systematic reviews suggest that focused or microfocused ultrasound can produce measurable improvement in suitable patients with mild-to-moderate facial laxity, although the visible change is generally modest and study protocols vary.

Who may be suitable for HIFU?

HIFU may be considered for an adult who:

  • Has mild or moderate skin looseness
  • Wants a non-surgical treatment
  • Understands that improvement develops gradually
  • Does not expect a surgical facelift result
  • Has no active infection or open wound in the treatment area
  • Is medically suitable for the specific device
  • Can follow treatment and aftercare instructions

Patients with severe laxity, substantial excess skin or major facial-volume loss may receive limited improvement from HIFU alone. The 2023 systematic review found that results tended to be less favourable when laxity was more advanced.

Which areas may be treated?

Depending on the patient’s anatomy and the indications of the particular device, HIFU may be considered for:

  • Lower face
  • Jawline
  • Area beneath the chin
  • Neck
  • Selected cheek areas
  • Selected brow or forehead concerns

Treatment near the eyes, major nerves, glands, bone or important blood vessels requires careful anatomical planning.

Treatment areas depend on the specific device, its instructions and the patient’s assessment.

Is HIFU painful?

HIFU is not completely painless for every patient.

Possible sensations include:

  • Tingling
  • Heat
  • Brief pinprick sensations
  • Deep aching
  • Tenderness over bony areas
  • Short electrical-like sensations

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis found moderate average procedural discomfort, while common short-term reactions included redness, swelling, bruising and tenderness.

Comfort varies according to treatment location, energy settings, anatomy and individual sensitivity.

Is anaesthesia required?

HIFU is usually performed without general anaesthesia.

Depending on the device, treatment area and patient sensitivity, the clinic may discuss:

  • No anaesthesia
  • Topical numbing treatment
  • Oral pain relief where medically suitable
  • Cooling or treatment modifications

Patients should not take pain-relieving or anti-inflammatory medicines before treatment unless advised, because their medical history and existing medicines must first be considered.

Is there downtime after HIFU?

Many patients return to routine activities after treatment.

Temporary effects may include:

  • Redness
  • Mild swelling
  • Tenderness
  • Tingling
  • Bruising
  • Temporary numbness
  • Sensitivity when touching the treated area

These effects are generally mild and temporary in published studies, although uncommon serious complications have been reported.

When will HIFU results become visible?

HIFU results are not usually immediate or dramatic.

The body requires time to remodel collagen. Improvement may become more visible over approximately two to six months, although the exact timeline varies.

Possible changes may include:

  • Mildly improved firmness
  • Softer appearance of early jowling
  • Improved lower-face definition
  • Reduced appearance of mild submental laxity
  • Gradual improvement in selected lines

The final result should be assessed with consistent photographs rather than day-to-day mirror checks.

How many HIFU sessions are required?

Some patients undergo one initial treatment followed by clinical review. Others may be advised to have an additional treatment depending on:

  • Device protocol
  • Degree of laxity
  • Treatment area
  • Age
  • Skin thickness
  • Previous procedures
  • Response to the first session
  • Maintenance goals

AAD guidance notes that many people receive one ultrasound treatment, while some may gain additional benefit from further sessions.

A fixed package should not be prescribed before examination.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
How long do HIFU results last?

The duration varies because:

  • Natural ageing continues
  • Collagen response differs
  • Sun exposure affects the skin
  • Smoking affects tissue quality
  • Weight changes alter facial contours

The treatment device and settings differ

The starting degree of laxity differs

Long-term evidence remains limited, and studies use different devices and follow-up periods. One systematic review noted that robust longer-term data beyond approximately one year were lacking in the included research.

Maintenance treatment may be discussed after the response has been reviewed.

Can HIFU replace a facelift?

No.

HIFU cannot:

  • Remove substantial excess skin
  • Reposition tissue as extensively as surgery
  • Produce a full surgical neck lift
  • Correct severe jowling
  • Permanently stop ageing
  • Guarantee a sharp jawline

Non-invasive skin-tightening procedures provide considerably less lifting than facelift, neck-lift or eyelid surgery.

A surgical opinion may be more appropriate when the patient wants major structural correction.

Facial anatomy is assessed first

The clinic evaluates skin laxity, facial volume and underlying structure before recommending treatment.

Realistic expectations

HIFU is presented as a gradual, non-surgical option—not as a facelift replacement.

Evidence-conscious wording

The clinic does not claim “latest technology,” “US-FDA-approved machine,” “painless treatment” or guaranteed results without device-specific evidence.

items.question: What are the risks of HIFU?
items.answer:
Temporary reactions may include:

  • Pain
  • Redness
  • Swelling
  • Bruising
  • Tenderness
  • Tingling
  • Numbness

Rare or more serious complications reported with microfocused-ultrasound treatment or device surveillance include:

  • Burns
  • Skin injury
  • Persistent altered sensation
  • Nerve-related symptoms
  • Scarring
  • Localised tissue or fat loss
  • Asymmetry
  • Unsatisfactory results

A 2025 systematic review found that serious events were uncommon in published studies but identified reports of lipoatrophy, neurological symptoms and scarring in device-reporting data.

items.question: Who may need to avoid or postpone HIFU?
items.answer:
Treatment may require postponement or additional review when there is:

  • Pregnancy or breastfeeding
  • Open wounds
  • Active skin infection
  • Severe inflammatory or cystic acne in the area
  • Active herpes
  • A pacemaker or implanted defibrillator
  • Metallic implants within the treatment area
  • Reduced sensation
  • Recent facial surgery
  • Recent filler or thread treatment
  • An uncontrolled medical condition
  • Unrealistic expectations

FDA guidance identifies open wounds, severe or cystic acne, active implanted devices and metallic implants among important contraindication considerations for focused-ultrasound devices.

The specific machine’s instructions must always take priority.

items.question: Can HIFU be performed after fillers or threads?
items.answer:
Previous fillers or threads must be disclosed.

The doctor may review:

  • Product used
  • Area treated
  • Treatment date
  • Injection depth
  • Previous complications
  • Thread location
  • Desired result

Treatment may need to be delayed, modified or performed in a different anatomical plane. HIFU should not be applied blindly over recently treated tissue.

items.question: Is HIFU suitable for Indian skin?
items.answer:
Focused ultrasound does not target melanin in the same way as pigment-specific lasers, so it may be considered across a range of skin tones.

However, it is not risk-free. Burns or inflammation can still produce:

  • Dark marks
  • Lighter patches
  • Prolonged redness
  • Scarring
  • Sensitivity

Skin tone, skin condition, treatment settings and aftercare remain important.

items.question: What aftercare may be recommended?
items.answer:
Patients may be advised to:

  • Use a gentle cleanser
  • Apply a simple moisturiser
  • Use sunscreen
  • Avoid excessive rubbing
  • Avoid strong exfoliating products temporarily
  • Avoid another energy-based procedure until advised
  • Report severe pain, blistering or persistent weakness
  • Attend the recommended review

The exact instructions depend on the treatment area, device and skin response.

value.heading: What is a Hydrafacial?
value.body:
“Hydrafacial” is commonly used to describe a hydradermabrasion-style facial procedure involving several steps, which may include:

  • Cleansing
  • Controlled exfoliation
  • Suction-assisted extraction
  • Application of hydrating solutions
  • Application of selected serums
  • Optional supportive steps according to the skin concern

Hydradermabrasion combines crystal-free surface exfoliation with pneumatic or suction-assisted application of skincare solutions. A small controlled study reported improvements in selected measures of skin quality after a course of treatment, although only 20 women participated.

Device details and regulatory claims depend on the exact system used and are discussed during consultation.

value.heading: What is a medifacial?
value.body:
A medifacial, or medical facial, is a broad term for a customised clinic-based facial planned according to the patient’s skin type and concern.

Depending on assessment, it may include a combination of:

  • Gentle cleansing
  • Enzyme or superficial exfoliation
  • Comedone care
  • Hydradermabrasion
  • Controlled suction
  • Hydrating masks
  • Suitable active serums
  • LED treatment where clinically appropriate
  • Moisturiser and sunscreen

There is no single universal medifacial protocol. A facial for dry, sensitive skin should not be identical to one designed for oily or congested skin.

value.heading: How is a medifacial different from a salon facial?
value.body:
A dermatologist-led medifacial begins with assessment of the skin rather than selection from a standard beauty menu.

The consultation may consider:

  • Active acne
  • Skin sensitivity
  • Rosacea
  • Eczema or dermatitis
  • Pigmentation tendency
  • Current medicines
  • Retinoid use
  • Recent peels or lasers
  • Pregnancy or breastfeeding
  • History of cold sores
  • Upcoming events

The aim is to avoid ingredients or steps that may aggravate an existing skin disorder. A facial should not be described as “medical” merely because stronger products are used.

value.heading: Which skin concerns may benefit?
value.body:
A customised facial may be considered for selected concerns such as:

  • Dry or dehydrated-looking skin
  • Dull complexion
  • Mild surface roughness
  • Oily skin
  • Congested pores
  • Blackheads
  • Mild comedonal acne
  • Temporary loss of radiance
  • Uneven-looking texture
  • Preparation for a special event
  • Maintenance between other dermatology procedures

The AAD states that controlled microdermabrasion can help selected patients with dullness, uneven texture, superficial dark marks and a less radiant complexion.

A facial cannot diagnose or permanently correct every concern in this list.

value.heading: What does current research show?
value.body:
Evidence for hydradermabrasion is more limited than the evidence available for many established medical treatments.

Published studies include:

A 20-participant trial reporting changes in fine lines, pore appearance, pigmentation and microscopic skin features after six hydradermabrasion sessions

An imaging study involving only eight volunteers

A 20-patient, open-label study of a branded clarifying protocol for mild-to-moderate acne

The acne study had no blinded control group, and an author was affiliated with the device company. These limitations mean results should be interpreted cautiously rather than promoted as proof that the treatment cures acne or permanently changes the skin.

value.heading: Can Hydrafacial help acne?
value.body:
A hydradermabrasion or clarifying facial may support selected patients with:

  • Mild comedonal acne
  • Blackheads
  • Whiteheads
  • Excess surface oil
  • Congested pores
  • Rough texture

A small open-label study involving 20 adults with mild-to-moderate acne reported improvement after six treatments over 12 weeks. However, the study was small, unblinded and included company involvement, so the procedure should be viewed as supportive care rather than a replacement for established acne treatment.

Inflammatory, nodular, cystic or scarring acne usually requires a dermatologist-directed medical plan.

value.heading: Can it remove blackheads?
value.body:
Suction and controlled exfoliation may temporarily clear some superficial pore contents and improve the appearance of congestion.

However:

  • Not every dark pore is a blackhead
  • Deep comedones may need separate extraction
  • Aggressive suction can irritate sensitive skin
  • Blackheads can return
  • Ongoing acne care may still be required

Repeated strong extraction should not be performed over inflamed acne, broken skin or fragile blood vessels.

value.heading: Can it improve dry or dehydrated-looking skin?
value.body:
Selected hydrating solutions and moisturising steps may improve the temporary appearance and feel of dry or dehydrated skin.

Patients may notice:

  • Softer-feeling skin
  • Temporary plumping
  • Smoother surface texture
  • Improved visible radiance
  • Better comfort after moisturising

Small studies of hydradermabrasion and serum-assisted microdermabrasion have reported short-term improvements in hydration and skin appearance, but protocols, products and funding sources vary.

Persistent dryness may instead result from eczema, irritation, over-exfoliation, medicines or an unsuitable skincare routine.

value.heading: Can Hydrafacial treat pigmentation or melasma?
value.body:
A superficial facial may temporarily improve overall brightness or help selected superficial dark marks appear less prominent.

It is not a stand-alone cure for:

  • Melasma
  • Deep pigmentation
  • Hormonal pigmentation
  • Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
  • Freckles
  • Sun-induced lentigines

AAD guidance notes that controlled microdermabrasion may support treatment of uneven tone, superficial dark marks and melasma in selected patients, generally as one part of a broader plan.

Melasma usually requires consistent sunscreen, suitable prescription skincare and long-term maintenance.

Related carePigmentation TreatmentMelasma Treatment

value.heading: Can a facial remove acne scars?
value.body:
No routine Hydrafacial or medifacial can remove deep acne scars.

It may temporarily improve:

  • Surface smoothness
  • Dryness around scars
  • Congestion
  • Post-acne dullness
  • Superficial dark marks

Rolling, boxcar, ice-pick and tethered scars may require procedures such as:

  • MNRF
  • Microneedling
  • Subcision
  • TCA CROSS
  • Fractional CO₂ laser
  • Combination scar treatment

value.heading: Can it reduce pores permanently?
value.body:
No treatment can permanently open, close or erase pores.

A facial may make pores appear temporarily less prominent by:

  • Removing some surface debris
  • Reducing congestion
  • Improving hydration
  • Smoothing the outer skin surface
  • Controlling excess oil as part of a wider plan

Pore appearance is also influenced by genetics, oil production, acne, skin elasticity and sun-related change.

value.heading: Can Hydrafacial remove wrinkles?
value.body:
Hydration and surface exfoliation may temporarily soften the appearance of very fine dehydration lines.

The treatment cannot:

  • Remove deep wrinkles
  • Relax expression muscles
  • Restore substantial facial volume
  • Lift significantly loose skin
  • Replace botulinum toxin
  • Replace fillers
  • Replace resurfacing procedures

An early small study reported improvements in fine-line appearance after a treatment course, but the evidence is not strong enough to promise wrinkle removal.

value.heading: How does Dr. Cheena Langer select the treatment?
value.body:
A consultation may include:

  • Identifying the patient’s main concern
  • Examining oiliness, dryness and sensitivity
  • Checking for active acne or infection
  • Looking for eczema, rosacea or dermatitis
  • Reviewing current skincare
  • Asking about retinoids and acne medicines
  • Reviewing recent peels, lasers or waxing
  • Checking pregnancy or breastfeeding status
  • Discussing expected benefits and limitations
  • Selecting or avoiding particular solutions and treatment steps

A facial may be postponed or replaced by medical treatment when an active skin disease is present.

The clinic checks for acne, sensitivity, pigmentation, rosacea, dermatitis and other conditions before selecting the facial steps.

Treatment is planned under Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist.

Dry, oily, acne-prone and sensitive skin are not given the same standard facial.

Patients with inflammatory acne, melasma, eczema or another diagnosed concern can be redirected to appropriate dermatology care.

The facial is presented as supportive cosmetic care—not as a detox, permanent pore treatment or cure for skin disease.

Hydrafacial and medifacial services are available at both Karan Nagar and Paloura.

Procedure cost depends on:

  • Facial protocol
  • Skin concern
  • Treatment duration
  • Products and solutions used
  • Whether extraction is included
  • Optional supportive steps
  • Face, neck or additional treatment area
  • Single session or treatment course

Exact pricing should be provided after assessment. A gentle hydration facial requires a different protocol from a clarifying facial for congested, acne-prone skin.

value.heading: How care is planned
value.body:
• Assessment comes before treatment selection.
  • Options, limitations, aftercare and expected timelines are explained.
  • The plan is adapted to diagnosis, skin type and medical history.

items.question: What happens during the treatment?
items.answer:
A customised appointment may involve:

  • Cleansing the skin
  • Examining the face under appropriate lighting
  • Performing controlled exfoliation
  • Applying a mild solution when suitable
  • Using suction-based cleansing or extraction
  • Applying selected hydrating or supportive serums
  • Using a calming mask or optional supportive treatment
  • Applying moisturiser
  • Applying sunscreen
  • Providing aftercare advice

Not every patient requires every step. Stronger or longer treatment is not automatically better.

items.question: What does the procedure feel like?
items.answer:
Patients may feel:

  • Coolness
  • Light suction
  • A wet or swirling sensation
  • Mild pressure
  • Gentle scratching or exfoliation
  • Temporary tingling from selected solutions

Controlled microdermabrasion is generally described as non-invasive, although temporary sensitivity can occur.

The treatment should not be advertised as completely sensation-free or painless for every patient.

items.question: Is there downtime?
items.answer:
Many patients resume ordinary activities after a superficial facial.

Temporary effects may include:

  • Mild redness
  • Tightness
  • Dryness
  • Temporary sensitivity
  • Mild swelling
  • Tingling
  • A short acne flare
  • Irritation from an active solution

AAD guidance for controlled microdermabrasion notes that redness or slight swelling can occur and may resemble mild windburn or sunburn for a day or two.

items.question: What complications are possible?
items.answer:
Possible complications include:

  • Irritation
  • Excessive redness
  • Burning
  • Bruising from suction
  • Broken superficial blood vessels
  • Acne flare
  • Contact dermatitis
  • Cold-sore reactivation
  • Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
  • Infection from poor hygiene
  • Aggravation of rosacea or eczema

People who tend to develop dark marks after inflammation may have a greater risk of post-procedure pigmentation.

The risk depends on skin sensitivity, products used, suction strength, technique and aftercare.

items.question: Who should postpone treatment?
items.answer:
A facial may need to be postponed or modified when there is:

  • Active bacterial, viral or fungal infection
  • Open wounds
  • Active cold sores
  • Sunburn
  • Significant dermatitis
  • A severe rosacea flare
  • Painful cystic acne
  • Recent facial surgery
  • A suspicious or changing skin growth
  • Recent strong peel or laser treatment
  • Severe skin-barrier damage
  • Known allergy to a planned ingredient

The AAD advises dermatologist assessment before microdermabrasion when a person has a growing or bleeding spot, scars easily or has used isotretinoin recently.

items.question: What about isotretinoin and acne medicines?
items.answer:
Patients should disclose:

  • Current isotretinoin use
  • Previous isotretinoin treatment
  • Prescription retinoids
  • Benzoyl peroxide
  • Salicylic acid
  • Glycolic acid
  • Antibiotic treatment
  • Other exfoliating medicines or skincare

AAD guidance warns that people taking or recently taking isotretinoin may have an increased complication risk from microdermabrasion and may need to delay treatment.

Products should only be paused when advised by the treating clinician.

items.question: Can treatment be performed during pregnancy?
items.answer:
A gentle facial may be possible during pregnancy, but the exact ingredients matter.

Some protocols may contain:

  • Salicylic acid
  • Retinoid-related ingredients
  • Strong exfoliating acids
  • Unverified boosters
  • Essential oils or fragrances
  • LED or device-based additions

Patients should tell the clinic that they are pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive so that the treatment can be modified or postponed.

No facial should be labelled “pregnancy safe” without reviewing every product and treatment step.

title: Ingrown Toenail Treatment & Nail Surgery in Jammu

search_description: Consult Dr. Cheena Langer for ingrown toenail treatment and nail surgery in Jammu. Appointments at Karan Nagar and Paloura.
introduction: Dermatologist-led assessment and personalised care for ingrown toenail treatment & nail surgery, available at Karan Nagar and Paloura Chowk.

value.heading: Treatment for painful, swollen and recurring ingrown toenails
value.body:
Consult Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist, for diagnosis-led ingrown toenail treatment and suitable nail surgery at Aastha Skin & Dermato-Cosmetic Centre in Jammu.

An ingrown toenail may begin as mild tenderness but can progress to swelling, overgrown tissue, discharge and infection. Treatment depends on its severity, duration, previous episodes and the patient’s medical history.

Ingrown-toenail assessment and nail surgery are available at both Karan Nagar and Paloura.

value.heading: What is an ingrown toenail?
value.body:
An ingrown toenail develops when the edge or corner of the nail presses into or grows through the adjoining skin.

It most commonly affects the big toe, although any toenail can be involved. The surrounding skin may become painful, red, swollen and inflamed. Pus or discharge can develop when infection is present.

The medical term for an ingrown nail is onychocryptosis.

value.heading: What are the symptoms of an ingrown toenail?
value.body:
Common symptoms include:

  • Pain along one or both sides of the nail
  • Tenderness when wearing shoes
  • Redness or darker inflammation around the nail
  • Swelling of the nail fold
  • Skin growing over the nail edge
  • Bleeding
  • Pus or discharge
  • Difficulty walking
  • Repeated infection
  • Unpleasant smell in advanced cases

A badly inflamed toe may also develop excess healing tissue, sometimes called granulation tissue, around the nail edge.

value.heading: What causes an ingrown toenail?
value.body:
Common contributing factors include:

  • Cutting toenails too short
  • Rounding or digging into the nail corners
  • Tight, narrow or pointed footwear
  • Repeated toe pressure
  • Sports-related trauma
  • Stubbing the toe
  • Naturally curved nails
  • Thickened nails
  • Sweaty feet
  • Improper pedicure techniques
  • Picking or tearing the nail
  • Previous nail injury

The NHS and AAOS recommend trimming toenails straight across and avoiding shoes that compress the toes.

value.heading: When should an ingrown toenail be examined?
value.body:
Arrange a medical assessment when:

  • Home care has not helped
  • Pain is increasing
  • Pus is present
  • The toe is significantly swollen
  • The problem keeps returning
  • Walking or footwear has become difficult
  • Overgrown tissue surrounds the nail
  • Both sides of the nail are affected
  • The patient has diabetes
  • Circulation or immunity is reduced
  • The diagnosis is uncertain
  • The nail is thick, damaged or discoloured

People with diabetes should seek medical advice earlier because infections and foot wounds can become more serious.

value.heading: How does Dr. Cheena Langer assess an ingrown toenail?
value.body:
A nail consultation may include:

  • Examining the nail edge and surrounding skin
  • Checking for pus, bleeding or infection
  • Assessing whether one or both sides are involved
  • Reviewing previous episodes and treatments
  • Checking the way the nail has been trimmed
  • Examining footwear-related pressure
  • Looking for nail fungus or thickening
  • Reviewing diabetes, circulation and medicines
  • Assessing scar and healing history
  • Deciding whether conservative treatment or surgery is appropriate

The diagnosis is usually clinical, but another condition may need to be considered when the appearance is unusual or treatment repeatedly fails.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Mild ingrown toenail

A mild case may cause tenderness and slight redness without pus or significant overgrowth of tissue.

Moderate ingrown toenail

The toe may become increasingly painful, swollen and inflamed. Discharge or early infection may develop.

Severe or recurrent ingrown toenail

There may be pronounced swelling, pus, bleeding, overgrown tissue or repeated episodes affecting the same nail edge.

Mild cases may respond to conservative care, while painful, infected or repeatedly recurring cases may require a procedure.

Can a mild ingrown toenail be treated without surgery?

Yes. Early cases may improve with conservative care.

Patients may be advised to:

  • Soak the foot in warm water
  • Dry the foot thoroughly afterwards
  • Wear wide, comfortable shoes or sandals
  • Avoid pressure on the affected toe
  • Allow the nail to grow
  • Avoid cutting into the sides
  • Use suitable pain relief after medical advice
  • Keep any discharge covered with a clean dressing
  • Return if symptoms worsen

The NHS recommends warm soaks, comfortable footwear and avoiding further cutting or picking of the nail.

People with diabetes, reduced circulation or reduced immunity should not attempt prolonged home treatment without medical guidance.

What should patients avoid?

Avoid:

  • Cutting a deep V-shape into the nail
  • Digging into the corners
  • Tearing off the nail edge
  • Using an unsterile blade
  • Repeated pedicure cutting
  • Wearing narrow shoes
  • Picking inflamed skin
  • Applying harsh acids or chemicals
  • Attempting home nail removal
  • Ignoring pus or spreading redness

Trying to cut out the embedded corner can injure the nail fold and encourage the nail to grow inward again.

Are antibiotics always needed?

No. Antibiotics are not automatically required for every ingrown toenail.

They may be considered when there are signs of bacterial infection, such as:

  • Pus
  • Spreading redness
  • Increasing warmth
  • Significant swelling
  • Fever
  • Cellulitis
  • Higher medical risk

Removing the nail edge that is repeatedly injuring the skin may still be necessary. Antibiotics alone do not correct the underlying nail shape or pressure. AAOS guidance notes that infected and severely inflamed ingrown nails may require both medical treatment and partial or complete nail removal.

What is nail surgery?

Nail surgery is a minor procedure used to treat a painful, recurrent or severely ingrown toenail.

The toe is numbed with local anaesthetic. Depending on the problem, the clinician may remove:

  • The problematic side of the nail
  • Both sides of the nail
  • A larger portion of the nail
  • The whole nail in selected cases
  • Part of the nail-producing matrix in recurrent cases

NHS patient guidance describes nail surgery as removal of part or all of a problematic nail under local anaesthetic.

The precise technique is selected after examination and consent.

What is partial nail avulsion?

Partial nail avulsion means removing only the narrow edge of the nail that is pressing into the skin.

It may be considered when:

  • One side is repeatedly ingrown
  • The rest of the nail is healthy
  • Pain keeps returning
  • Overgrown tissue has developed
  • Conservative treatment has failed

The toe is numbed before the embedded nail section is separated and removed. The remaining central nail is left in place.

Partial removal usually preserves more of the nail’s normal appearance than complete removal.

Diagnosis before surgery

The nail and surrounding tissue are examined to determine whether the concern is an ingrown nail, infection, fungus, trauma or another nail disorder.

Conservative and procedural options

Mild cases may receive non-surgical guidance, while recurrent or severe cases may be considered for suitable nail surgery.

Infection and medical-risk assessment

Diabetes, medicines, circulation, infection and healing risk are reviewed when relevant.

items.question: When is complete nail removal considered?
items.answer:
Complete nail removal may be considered when:

  • Both sides are severely affected
  • The nail is extensively damaged
  • The nail is significantly thickened or distorted
  • Previous partial procedures have failed
  • Another nail disorder requires removal
  • The entire nail plate is contributing to pain

Removing the whole nail is not necessary for every patient. AAOS notes that complete nail removal can increase the possibility of abnormal regrowth, so the benefits and limitations should be discussed carefully.

items.question: What is treatment of the nail matrix?
items.answer:
The nail matrix is the tissue that produces the nail.

For a repeatedly ingrown nail edge, part of the matrix may be treated so that the troublesome strip is less likely to grow back. This may involve an appropriate chemical or surgical technique.

NHS nail-surgery guidance describes the use of phenol after removal of the affected nail section to reduce regrowth of that particular edge.

The clinic page should not promise that recurrence is impossible. Regrowth can still occur in a small proportion of patients.

items.question: Is ingrown toenail surgery painful?
items.answer:
The local-anaesthetic injection may briefly sting or feel uncomfortable.

Once the toe is adequately numb, the patient should not feel sharp pain during the procedure, although pressure or movement may still be noticeable. More anaesthetic can be given when required.

Mild soreness may develop after the anaesthetic wears off. Pain levels vary according to:

  • Extent of surgery
  • Infection and inflammation
  • Individual sensitivity
  • Dressing pressure
  • Activity after treatment
  • Healing response

The website should not describe nail surgery as completely painless.

items.question: How should patients prepare for nail surgery?
items.answer:
Before treatment, patients should disclose:

  • Diabetes
  • Poor circulation
  • Bleeding disorders
  • Blood-thinning medicines
  • Allergies
  • Previous reaction to local anaesthesia
  • Pregnancy or breastfeeding
  • Current antibiotics
  • Fever or acute illness
  • Previous nail surgery
  • Difficulty healing wounds

Patients may also be advised to:

  • Wash the foot
  • Avoid applying nail polish
  • Wear loose footwear or sandals
  • Arrange transport if necessary
  • Bring a list of medicines
  • Eat normally unless instructed otherwise

Do not stop prescribed medicines independently.

items.question: What happens after nail surgery?
items.answer:
A dressing is applied after the procedure.

Patients may experience:

  • Mild pain or throbbing
  • Temporary bleeding
  • Clear or blood-stained discharge
  • Swelling
  • Tenderness
  • Difficulty wearing closed shoes
  • Gradual crusting and healing

Instructions may include:

  • Resting and elevating the foot initially
  • Keeping the dressing clean
  • Changing dressings as instructed
  • Wearing open or roomy footwear
  • Avoiding pressure on the toe
  • Using advised pain relief
  • Returning for follow-up
  • Reporting worsening pain, pus or fever

NHS guidance advises keeping a discharging ingrown nail covered with a clean, dry dressing and following wound-care instructions after surgery.

items.question: How long does recovery take?
items.answer:
Recovery depends on:

  • Whether part or all of the nail was removed
  • Whether the matrix was treated
  • Presence of infection
  • Medical conditions
  • Footwear and daily activity
  • Wound care
  • Individual healing response

The wound can continue to release a small amount of fluid while healing. Returning to work or routine activity depends on comfort, occupation and the amount of standing or walking involved.

If the nail is allowed to regrow, regrowth takes months. Toenails grow slowly, and complete regrowth after removal can take considerably longer than fingernail regrowth.

items.question: What are the possible risks of nail surgery?
items.answer:
Potential risks include:

  • Pain
  • Bleeding
  • Infection
  • Delayed healing
  • Nail regrowth
  • Irregular nail growth
  • Permanent narrowing of the nail
  • Pigmentation change
  • Scarring
  • Reaction to local anaesthetic
  • Rare nerve-related symptoms

The expected cosmetic appearance should be discussed before matrix treatment because the treated nail may remain permanently narrower.

title: IPL Photofacial Treatment in Jammu
seo_title: IPL Photofacial in Jammu | Aastha Skin Centre
search_description: Explore dermatologist-led IPL photofacial treatment for facial redness, visible vessels and selected sun spots in Jammu. Book a consultation.
introduction: Dermatologist-led assessment and personalised care for ipl photofacial, available at Karan Nagar and Paloura Chowk.

value.heading: What is IPL?
value.body:
IPL stands for intense pulsed light.

An IPL device produces broad-spectrum, non-coherent light rather than the single focused wavelength associated with many medical lasers. Filters and treatment settings are used to direct selected wavelengths towards targets such as:

  • Melanin in brown pigmentation
  • Oxyhaemoglobin in visible blood vessels
  • Selected signs of sun-related skin change

Absorbed light is converted into heat within the intended target. The body then gradually clears or remodels the treated structures.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Is IPL a laser?

No. IPL and laser treatment are both light-based procedures, but they are not identical.

Produces a range of wavelengths

Uses filters to select part of that light spectrum

Can address more than one suitable skin target

Usually treats a relatively broad surface area

  • Generally produces a more specific wavelength
  • May target one selected pigment, vessel or tissue depth
  • Has indications that depend on the particular laser

One treatment is not automatically superior. The appropriate choice depends on the diagnosis, skin tone, treatment target and device available.

What does “photofacial” mean?

Photofacial or photorejuvenation is a commonly used term for light-based facial treatment intended to improve selected visible signs of sun exposure, redness or uneven colour.

It does not mean that the treatment:

  • Replaces a surgical facelift
  • Removes every pigmentation concern
  • Permanently stops ageing
  • Treats every form of facial redness
  • Produces the same result in every patient

“Photofacial” is a broad description. The patient should be told whether the planned procedure specifically uses IPL and what concern it is intended to treat.

Which concerns may IPL photofacial address?

After examination, IPL may be considered for selected concerns including:

  • Persistent facial redness
  • Visible superficial blood vessels
  • Telangiectasia
  • Selected rosacea-related redness
  • Sun spots
  • Solar lentigines
  • Freckle-like superficial pigmentation
  • Uneven sun-related colour
  • Selected signs of photodamage
  • Mild surface-texture concerns

A systematic review involving 16 studies and 637 participants reported improvement across concerns such as telangiectasia, erythema, lentigines, hyperpigmentation and skin texture. However, nine studies were rated as having low methodological quality, so benefits should be described realistically.

Can IPL treat facial redness?

IPL may help reduce selected facial redness when dilated superficial vessels or vascular colour contribute to the concern.

A systematic review and meta-analysis involving seven studies found that IPL improved facial erythema compared with no treatment. Outcomes were broadly similar to pulsed-dye laser in the comparative studies, although the authors called for larger, higher-quality research.

Redness should be diagnosed first because it may also result from:

  • Rosacea
  • Acne
  • Contact dermatitis
  • Eczema
  • Sunburn
  • Steroid use
  • Infection
  • Lupus or another medical condition

Can IPL help rosacea?

IPL may be included in a rosacea-treatment plan for persistent facial colour, flushing or visible vessels in suitable patients.

Rosacea care may also require:

  • Trigger management
  • Gentle cleansing
  • Moisturiser
  • Daily sun protection
  • Prescription topical treatment
  • Oral treatment in selected cases
  • Eye assessment when ocular symptoms are present

The American Academy of Dermatology states that IPL can reduce flushing and improve texture, but it generally requires several sessions and should be combined with appropriate skincare and medical treatment when needed.

IPL controls selected visible signs; it does not permanently cure rosacea.

Can IPL treat visible facial blood vessels?

Yes, selected small superficial vessels may respond because the light can be absorbed by haemoglobin within the vessel.

Treatment may be considered for:

  • Telangiectasia
  • Fine vessels around the nose
  • Diffuse cheek redness
  • Selected post-inflammatory vascular marks
  • Sun-related vascular changes

In a randomised split-face study, IPL improved telangiectasia and irregular pigmentation, although the improvement was mainly mild or moderate and one scar was reported among the participants.

Large, deep or blue vessels may require another vascular treatment.

Can IPL treat brown spots?

IPL may help selected superficial brown spots that contain excess melanin, including some sun-related lentigines and freckle-like pigmentation.

The response depends on:

  • Type of pigmentation
  • Depth of pigment
  • Skin tone
  • Recent sun exposure
  • Treatment filter and settings
  • Presence of melasma
  • Tendency to develop dark marks

Brown spots should be examined before treatment. A changing, irregular, bleeding or unusual lesion should not be treated cosmetically until a dermatologist has excluded a suspicious growth.

Is IPL suitable for melasma?

IPL is not a routine first treatment for every patient with melasma.

Melasma is chronic, frequently recurs and is particularly common in people with medium-to-deep skin tones. Although IPL has been studied as part of combination therapy, results are variable and heat or inflammation can worsen pigmentation in some patients.

Treatment usually begins with:

  • Diagnosis confirmation
  • Broad-spectrum sunscreen
  • Visible-light protection where appropriate
  • Prescription depigmenting treatment
  • Trigger management
  • Long-term maintenance

IPL should only be considered when Dr. Cheena Langer believes the pigmentation pattern, skin tone and risk profile are suitable.

Can IPL treat post-acne marks?

IPL may help when post-acne marks contain a combination of superficial brown pigmentation or persistent vascular redness.

It does not treat every post-acne concern equally.

It may support treatment for

  • Selected red post-acne marks
  • Superficial brown marks
  • Uneven colour after acne

It does not adequately treat

  • Deep rolling scars
  • Boxcar scars
  • Ice-pick scars
  • Tethered scars
  • Active nodular acne

People with darker skin tones have a greater tendency to develop post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and light-based treatment itself can occasionally worsen it.

  • Acne Treatment in Jammu
  • Acne Scar Treatment in Jammu
  • Pigmentation Treatment in Jammu

Can IPL improve wrinkles or loose skin?

IPL may improve selected aspects of photodamaged skin, particularly uneven pigmentation, superficial vessels and texture.

Its effect on deeper wrinkles or skin laxity is limited. In one randomised controlled trial, IPL improved texture, telangiectasia and irregular pigmentation but did not produce significant improvement in wrinkles.

IPL does not replace:

  • Botulinum toxin for expression lines
  • Dermal fillers for volume loss
  • HIFU or RF for selected laxity
  • Fractional resurfacing for deeper texture
  • Surgical lifting for substantial loose skin

Is IPL the same as LED therapy?

IPL

  • Uses high-intensity pulses
  • Produces controlled heating
  • Targets pigment or blood vessels
  • Requires eye protection
  • Can cause burns or pigment changes

LED or photobiomodulation

  • Uses much lower-intensity light
  • Does not use the same target-destruction mechanism
  • Has different indications and risks

The two terms should not be used interchangeably.

How does Dr. Cheena Langer assess IPL suitability?

An IPL consultation may include:

  • Confirming the patient’s main concern
  • Diagnosing the cause of redness or pigmentation
  • Assessing the patient’s natural skin tone
  • Checking for tanning or recent sun exposure
  • Reviewing previous dark marks after injury
  • Examining moles and other pigmented lesions
  • Reviewing active acne, rosacea or dermatitis
  • Checking medicines and supplements
  • Asking about photosensitivity
  • Reviewing previous lasers or IPL sessions
  • Discussing realistic improvement and possible risks
  • Considering a test spot

The same filter and energy settings should not be used automatically for every face.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
Why does skin tone matter?

IPL energy can be absorbed by both the intended pigment and the normal melanin in surrounding skin.

When the skin contains more melanin, there may be a higher risk of:

  • Excessive heat absorption
  • Burns
  • Blistering
  • Post-inflammatory darkening
  • Loss of natural skin colour
  • Uneven results

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is more common and can be more persistent in darker skin tones.

This does not mean IPL is impossible for every Indian patient. It means diagnosis, device selection, conservative settings and aftercare require particular care.

Why should IPL not be performed on recently tanned skin?

A tan increases melanin within the skin, creating greater competition between normal skin pigment and the intended treatment target.

This can raise the risk of:

  • Burns
  • Blisters
  • Dark marks
  • Light patches
  • Uneven response

FDA guidance for high-energy light procedures advises particular caution in patients who are tanned, planning significant sun exposure, prone to dark marks or taking photosensitising medicines.

Treatment may be postponed until the tan has faded.

Diagnosis before light treatment

Redness and pigmentation are assessed before selecting IPL so that dermatitis, melasma, infection or a suspicious growth is not treated as a simple cosmetic concern.

Careful assessment of Indian skin tones

Skin tone, tanning, pigmentation tendency and previous reactions are considered before treatment.

Technology recorded in the clinic inventory

IPL/photofacial technology is listed as available in the verified equipment inventory.

Realistic expectations

The clinic does not promise complete removal, painless treatment or identical results for every patient.

No unsupported device claims

Device details and regulatory claims depend on the exact system used and are discussed during consultation.

Need help choosing?

Facial redness and brown spots need diagnosis before light treatment

Request a dermatologist-led assessment at Karan Nagar or Paloura Chowk.

Book an appointmentWhatsApp the clinicCall 7006613362

Dermatology consultations can be booked at either Aastha Skin Centre branch. Reception will confirm the active IPL-procedure location and treatment slot.

IPL treatment cost depends on:

  • Condition being treated
  • Treatment area
  • Size of the area
  • Filter and device protocol
  • Number of sessions
  • Need for a test spot
  • Facial or non-facial treatment
  • Combination with medical skincare
  • Maintenance plan

Exact pricing is provided after assessment. Diffuse facial redness requires a different treatment plan from a small number of isolated brown spots.

value.heading: How care is planned
value.body:
• Assessment comes before treatment selection.
  • Options, limitations, aftercare and expected timelines are explained.
  • The plan is adapted to diagnosis, skin type and medical history.

items.question: Which medicines and conditions should patients disclose?
items.answer:
Tell Dr. Cheena Langer about:

  • Medicines that increase light sensitivity
  • Recent isotretinoin use
  • Blood-thinning medicines
  • Previous abnormal scarring
  • Keloid tendency
  • History of cold sores
  • Lupus or another photosensitivity disorder
  • Seizures triggered by flashing light
  • Diabetes
  • Reduced immunity
  • Pregnancy or breastfeeding
  • Previous skin cancer
  • Recent laser, peel or injectable treatment

Do not stop a prescribed medicine independently. The treatment decision should be made after medical review.

items.question: Who may need to postpone IPL?
items.answer:
Treatment may be postponed or modified when there is:

  • Recent tanning or sunburn
  • Active skin infection
  • Open wounds
  • Active cold sores
  • Severe dermatitis
  • A major rosacea flare
  • Uncontrolled inflammatory acne
  • Suspicious pigmented growths
  • Significant photosensitivity
  • Use of certain photosensitising medicines
  • Poor wound healing
  • Unrealistic expectations

The instructions for the particular IPL device must also be reviewed before treatment.

items.question: What happens during an IPL photofacial?
items.answer:
A typical appointment may involve:

  • Confirming and photographing the treatment area
  • Cleansing the skin
  • Covering or excluding unsuitable lesions
  • Providing protective eyewear
  • Applying cooling or conductive gel where required
  • Selecting an appropriate filter and settings
  • Delivering controlled pulses across planned areas
  • Monitoring the skin response after each pulse
  • Cooling or soothing the treated skin
  • Applying moisturiser and sunscreen
  • Providing written aftercare instructions

IPL is a high-powered light treatment, so appropriate patient and operator eye protection is essential. FDA-recognised standards specifically address protective eyewear for intense-light procedures.

items.question: What does IPL feel like?
items.answer:
Patients may feel:

  • Bright flashes behind the eye protection
  • Warmth
  • Brief stinging
  • A snapping sensation
  • Pinprick discomfort
  • Heat over darker spots
  • Temporary tenderness

Discomfort varies with the area, settings, cooling and individual sensitivity.

A clinical trial reported treatment-related pain significant enough for three participants to withdraw, illustrating why the procedure should not be promoted as completely painless.

items.question: Is anaesthesia required?
items.answer:
Many IPL photofacial treatments are performed without injectable anaesthesia.

Comfort measures may include:

  • Contact cooling
  • Cooling gel
  • Cold-air support
  • Treatment-setting adjustment
  • Smaller treatment sections
  • Topical anaesthesia when appropriate for the device and indication

The patient should immediately report sharp pain, intense focal heat or burning.

items.question: Is there downtime after IPL?
items.answer:
Many patients return to ordinary activities after treatment, but temporary skin changes are common.

These may include:

  • Redness
  • Mild swelling
  • Warmth
  • Tenderness
  • Temporary darkening of brown spots
  • Fine crusting
  • Mild bruising around vessels
  • Dryness or sensitivity

The degree of downtime depends on the condition treated, skin tone, treatment energy and individual response.

items.question: What side effects and complications are possible?
items.answer:
Possible adverse effects include:

  • Pain or discomfort
  • Redness
  • Swelling
  • Bruising
  • Blisters
  • Burns
  • Crusting
  • Dark pigmentation
  • Light pigmentation
  • Infection
  • Scarring
  • Unsatisfactory clearance
  • Eye injury if protection is inadequate

FDA information on high-energy light devices identifies burns, blisters, skin-colour changes and eye injury among recognised risks. Serious IPL burns have also been reported after unsuitable settings or operator error.
