title: Keloid & Hypertrophic Scar Treatment in Jammu
seo_title: Keloid & Hypertrophic Scar Treatment in Jammu
search_description: Get dermatologist-led care for raised, itchy or painful keloid and hypertrophic scars in Jammu. Book with Dr. Cheena Langer.
introduction: Dermatologist-led assessment and personalised care for keloid & hypertrophic scar, available at Karan Nagar and Paloura Chowk.

value.heading: What is a hypertrophic scar?
value.body:
A hypertrophic scar is a thick, raised scar that remains confined to the area of the original injury.

It may appear:

  • Red, pink, purple, brown or darker than nearby skin
  • Raised and firm
  • Itchy
  • Tender
  • Tight
  • Sensitive to pressure
  • Less flexible than surrounding skin

Hypertrophic scars may gradually flatten and soften over time, although improvement can take many months.

value.heading: What is a keloid?
value.body:
A keloid is an overgrown scar that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound.

It may continue growing after the skin has healed and can become substantially larger than the injury that triggered it. Keloids may develop weeks, months or even years after a cut, burn, acne lesion, operation or piercing.

value.heading: What is the difference between a keloid and a hypertrophic scar?
value.body:
• Stays within the original wound
  • Commonly appears soon after injury
  • May gradually flatten
  • Can remain red, thick or itchy
  • Often responds more predictably to treatment
  • Extends beyond the original wound
  • May continue growing for months or years
  • Is less likely to flatten naturally
  • Has a stronger tendency to recur
  • Often requires combination treatment

The distinction affects treatment choice, expected response and recurrence counselling.

value.heading: What causes raised scars?
value.body:
Raised scars develop when wound healing produces excess collagen and disorganised scar tissue within the deeper skin.

Potential triggers include:

  • Surgery
  • Burns
  • Cuts
  • Acne
  • Chickenpox
  • Vaccinations
  • Ear piercing
  • Tattoos
  • Insect bites
  • Skin infections
  • Caesarean-section wounds
  • Trauma
  • Minor scratches in susceptible people

Keloids can occasionally follow surprisingly small injuries.

value.heading: What symptoms can a keloid cause?
value.body:
A keloid may cause:

  • Itching
  • Burning
  • Tenderness
  • Pain
  • Tightness
  • Sensitivity to clothing
  • Reduced movement when close to a joint
  • Emotional distress
  • Difficulty wearing earrings
  • Irritation from shaving

Symptoms can continue while the keloid is active and growing.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Can a hypertrophic scar turn into a keloid?

No.

They are related forms of excessive scarring but behave differently. A hypertrophic scar does not later “convert” into a keloid. A scar that continues spreading beyond the original wound may have been a keloid from the beginning or may need reassessment.

Where do keloids commonly develop?

Frequent sites include:

  • Earlobes
  • Chest
  • Shoulders
  • Upper back
  • Jawline
  • Neck
  • Cheeks
  • Upper arms
  • Areas of piercing
  • Surgical scars

Keloids can occur on almost any injured area, but the palms, soles and eyelids are less commonly affected.

Are keloids dangerous?

Keloids are benign and do not spread through the body like cancer.

They can still cause significant problems when they:

  • Become painful
  • Itch continuously
  • Restrict joint movement
  • Interfere with clothing
  • Repeatedly become irritated
  • Grow after every attempted removal
  • Cause distress about appearance

A rapidly changing, ulcerated or bleeding lesion should be checked because another condition may resemble a raised scar.

Are keloids contagious?

No.

Keloids cannot spread through:

  • Touching
  • Towels
  • Clothing
  • Kissing
  • Swimming
  • Sexual contact
  • Sharing a bed
  • Living in the same household

They are an abnormal wound-healing response, not a bacterial, fungal or viral infection.

Who is more likely to develop keloids?

Risk is higher in people who:

  • Have previously developed a keloid
  • Have relatives with keloids
  • Have South Asian, African, Caribbean, Chinese or other melanin-rich ancestry
  • Are between approximately 10 and 30 years of age
  • Develop acne or injuries on high-risk body sites
  • Undergo piercing or elective skin procedures
  • Experience prolonged wound inflammation

Keloids can occur in any skin tone, but they are more frequent and often more noticeable in brown and black skin.

How do keloids appear on Indian skin?

On Indian skin, a keloid may appear:

  • Skin-coloured
  • Pink-brown
  • Red-brown
  • Purple
  • Dark brown
  • Shinier than nearby skin
  • Surrounded by pigmentation

Treatment can also produce dark or pale marks. Corticosteroid injections may occasionally cause lighter skin, while cryotherapy carries a meaningful risk of lasting pale pigmentation in darker skin tones.

Do keloids run in families?

They can.

A family history suggests inherited susceptibility to excessive scar formation. Patients should tell surgeons, dentists, dermatologists and piercing professionals when they or a close relative have developed keloids.

This information can influence wound closure, scar prevention and whether an elective procedure should be avoided.

Can acne cause keloids?

Yes.

Deep inflammatory acne can lead to:

  • Hypertrophic scars
  • Papular raised scars
  • Keloids
  • Dark post-inflammatory marks
  • Depressed scars occurring alongside raised scars

Raised acne scars require a different approach from indented acne scars. Early treatment of active acne can reduce the likelihood of additional scarring.

Can ear piercing cause keloids?

Yes.

Earlobe and cartilage piercings are common triggers in susceptible patients. Early signs may include:

  • Thickening around the piercing
  • Increasing firmness
  • Itching
  • A bump that continues enlarging
  • Extension beyond the original piercing hole

Early assessment may allow pressure treatment or injections to be considered before the lesion becomes large.

Should someone with a keloid get another piercing or tattoo?

Usually, extra caution is advisable.

A person who has already formed a keloid has a higher risk of developing another after:

  • Piercing
  • Tattooing
  • Cosmetic surgery
  • Elective skin procedures
  • Unnecessary mole removal
  • Permanent makeup

Avoiding non-essential skin injury is the most reliable form of prevention for strongly keloid-prone patients.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
Can a caesarean-section scar become raised?

Yes.

A C-section scar may become hypertrophic or, less commonly, develop keloidal overgrowth.

Assessment considers:

  • Whether the scar extends beyond the incision
  • Pain or itching
  • Width and thickness
  • Previous infection
  • Tension across the wound
  • Pregnancy or breastfeeding status
  • Future pregnancy plans

Treatment may include silicone, injections or another scar-directed approach after the wound has completely healed.

Can burns cause hypertrophic scars?

Yes.

Burn injuries are a common cause of hypertrophic scarring, particularly when healing is prolonged or the wound extends deeply into the skin.

Burn scars can also cause:

  • Tightness
  • Reduced movement
  • Contractures
  • Itching
  • Pain
  • Pigment changes

Scars limiting a joint or causing a contracture may require coordinated dermatology, plastic-surgery, physiotherapy or burn-specialist care.

Can keloids develop without an obvious injury?

Occasionally, the triggering injury may have been so minor that the patient does not remember it.

Possible unnoticed triggers include:

  • Small acne lesions
  • Insect bites
  • Folliculitis
  • Minor scratches
  • Shaving injury
  • A small vaccination site
  • A previously inflamed hair follicle

A lesion with no convincing injury history may require closer examination or biopsy to confirm that it is truly a keloid.

Keloid and hypertrophic-scar differentiation

The scar is assessed to determine whether it stays within or extends beyond the original wound.

Symptoms assessed alongside appearance

Pain, itching, tightness and restricted movement are included in treatment planning.

Indian-skin considerations

The risk of darkening, lightening and treatment-related pigmentation is considered before injections, cryotherapy or laser.

Biopsy when needed

Skin biopsy is available at both branches for atypical or uncertain raised lesions.

Appropriate referral

Large, recurrent or surgically complex keloids may be referred for plastic-surgical or radiation-oncology care.

Realistic expectations

The clinic does not promise complete, scar-free or permanent removal.

Need help choosing?

A raised scar that is growing, itching or painful should be assessed before it is cut, burned or injected

Request a dermatologist-led assessment at Karan Nagar or Paloura Chowk.

Book an appointmentWhatsApp the clinicCall 7006613362

General dermatology, fractional CO₂ laser, MNRF and skin biopsy are confirmed at both locations. Keloid injections, cryotherapy, excision and other scar-specific procedures should be confirmed after consultation.

Additional cost depends on:

  • Whether the scar is hypertrophic or keloidal
  • Scar size and thickness
  • Number of scars
  • Body area
  • Silicone treatment
  • Injection medicine
  • Number of injection sessions
  • Laser or another procedure
  • Biopsy in an uncertain case
  • Surgical referral
  • Pressure earrings or garments
  • Follow-up after the included 10-day period

An exact quote requires examination because a small earlobe scar requires different care from a large recurrent chest or post-burn keloid.

value.heading: How care is planned
value.body:
• Assessment comes before treatment selection.
  • Options, limitations, aftercare and expected timelines are explained.
  • The plan is adapted to diagnosis, skin type and medical history.

items.question: Is every raised scar a keloid?
items.answer:
No.

Possible alternatives include:

  • Hypertrophic scar
  • Dermatofibroma
  • Cyst
  • Foreign-body reaction
  • Infected piercing
  • Allergic reaction to jewellery
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Benign skin growth
  • Rarely, a skin tumour

A contact reaction to jewellery can occasionally mimic swelling around an ear piercing. Biopsy may be used when the diagnosis remains uncertain.

items.question: How does Dr. Cheena Langer assess a raised scar?
items.answer:
A consultation may include:

  • Reviewing the original injury
  • Examining whether growth extends beyond the wound
  • Measuring scar height and surface area
  • Assessing colour, firmness and flexibility
  • Asking about pain, itch and burning
  • Checking whether movement is restricted
  • Reviewing earlier injections or surgery
  • Asking about family history
  • Checking for active acne or infection
  • Assessing skin tone and pigmentation risk
  • Considering clinical photographs with consent
  • Considering biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain

A dermatologist can usually diagnose a keloid clinically.

items.question: When is a biopsy required?
items.answer:
Biopsy may be considered when:

  • The diagnosis is uncertain
  • The lesion is unusually hard or irregular
  • It grows rapidly
  • It bleeds or ulcerates
  • It appears without a clear injury
  • Treatment repeatedly fails
  • Another inflammatory condition or tumour is possible

Skin biopsy is confirmed as available at both Aastha Skin Centre branches when clinically required.

items.question: Do keloids disappear naturally?
items.answer:
Keloids usually do not disappear without treatment.

They may eventually stop growing and become less symptomatic, but the raised tissue generally remains. Hypertrophic scars have a greater tendency to flatten and soften over time.

items.question: Can keloids be permanently cured?
items.answer:
No treatment can guarantee permanent cure.

Treatment may:

  • Flatten the scar
  • Soften it
  • Reduce redness or darkness
  • Relieve pain and itching
  • Improve movement
  • Make it less noticeable
  • Reduce further growth

Recurrence remains possible, especially after surgical removal. Combination treatment is often used because keloids respond unpredictably.

items.question: Does every raised scar need treatment?
items.answer:
No.

Observation may be reasonable when the scar:

  • Is small and stable
  • Causes no pain or itch
  • Does not restrict movement
  • Does not bother the patient
  • Has a clear benign diagnosis

Earlier treatment may be considered when a scar is actively thickening, painful, itchy or extending beyond the original wound.

items.question: How are keloids and hypertrophic scars treated?
items.answer:
A treatment plan may include:

  • Silicone gel or silicone sheets
  • Pressure therapy
  • Corticosteroid injections
  • Another intralesional medicine
  • Cryotherapy
  • Laser or light treatment
  • Surgical removal with recurrence prevention
  • Specialist post-operative radiation in selected cases
  • Combination treatment

No single option is ideal for every scar. Size, site, symptoms, skin tone and previous treatment determine the plan.

title: Laser Hair Reduction in Jammu
seo_title: Laser Hair Reduction in Jammu | Aastha Skin Centre
search_description: Explore laser hair reduction in Jammu with Dr. Cheena Langer at Karan Nagar or Paloura. Call or WhatsApp to book.
introduction: Dermatologist-led assessment and personalised care for laser hair reduction, available at Karan Nagar and Paloura Chowk.

value.heading: Dermatologist-led reduction of unwanted facial and body hair
value.body:
Consult Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist, for personalised laser hair reduction at Aastha Skin & Dermato-Cosmetic Centre in Jammu.

Treatment is planned according to your skin tone, hair colour, hair thickness, treatment area, medical history and hormonal factors. Laser hair reduction is available at both the Karan Nagar and Paloura branches.

value.heading: What is laser hair reduction?
value.body:
Laser hair reduction is a medical-grade procedure that uses concentrated light to target pigment within suitable hair follicles.

The absorbed energy heats the follicle and can reduce its ability to produce coarse hair. Regrowing hair commonly becomes less dense, finer and lighter after a course of treatment.

The treatment is called laser hair reduction because:

  • Not every follicle responds equally
  • Hair grows in different cycles
  • Hormonal factors can cause new growth
  • Maintenance sessions may be needed
  • Complete lifelong removal of every hair cannot be promised

FDA device documentation defines permanent hair reduction as a long-term, stable reduction in regrowing hair—not necessarily the complete disappearance of every hair.

value.heading: How does laser hair reduction work?
value.body:
Hair contains melanin, the pigment that gives it colour. The laser produces light that is absorbed by this pigment and converted into heat.

That heat affects the hair follicle while the surrounding skin is protected through suitable treatment settings and cooling methods.

The response depends on:

  • Hair colour
  • Hair thickness
  • Skin tone
  • Body area
  • Hair-growth stage
  • Laser parameters
  • Hormonal influences
  • Previous hair-removal methods

Hair follicles respond most effectively when they are in an active growth phase. Because all hairs are not active at the same time, treatment must be repeated.

value.heading: Who may benefit from laser hair reduction?
value.body:
Laser treatment may be considered by people who:

  • Are tired of frequent shaving or waxing
  • Develop razor bumps
  • Experience recurrent ingrown hairs
  • Have coarse unwanted facial or body hair
  • Develop irritation after conventional hair removal
  • Want longer-term reduction in hair density
  • Have dark, visible hair suitable for laser targeting

A consultation is required because not every patient or hair type will respond equally.

value.heading: What happens during the first consultation?
value.body:
Before treatment, Dr. Cheena Langer or the clinical team may assess:

  • Skin tone
  • Hair colour and thickness
  • Treatment area
  • Hair-removal history
  • Recent sun exposure or tanning
  • Medicines and supplements
  • History of pigmentation or scarring
  • Active skin infections
  • Hormonal symptoms
  • Previous laser response

The AAD recommends disclosing recent tanning, keloid tendency, recurrent herpes, isotretinoin use and other medicines before laser treatment.

A test spot may be considered when clinically appropriate.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Why are multiple laser sessions required?

Hair grows through different biological stages. Only a proportion of hairs are in the most responsive growth stage during one appointment.

For this reason, laser hair reduction is performed as a planned course rather than a single treatment.

The American Academy of Dermatology notes that patients often require several sessions, commonly between two and six or more depending on the body area and individual response. Regrowth after treatment is generally finer and less noticeable, and maintenance may later be required.

The exact schedule is decided after assessing:

  • Treatment area
  • Density of hair
  • Hair thickness
  • Skin response
  • Hormonal pattern
  • Previous sessions

Which areas can be treated?

Laser hair reduction may be used for suitable facial and body areas.

  • Upper lip
  • Chin
  • Sideburns
  • Jawline
  • Neck
  • Full face
  • Underarms
  • Arms
  • Forearms
  • Shoulders
  • Chest
  • Abdomen
  • Back
  • Bikini line
  • Legs
  • Thighs
  • Lower legs
  • Toes
  • Full body

The AAD lists the face, underarms, chest, back, shoulders, neck, bikini area and legs among commonly treated areas.

Treatment should not be performed too close to the eyes or over unsuitable skin lesions without medical assessment.

Which hair colours respond best?

Laser hair reduction generally works best when there is sufficient pigment in the hair.

Dark, coarse hair often absorbs laser energy more effectively than fine or lightly pigmented hair.

Laser treatment responds poorly to:

  • White hair
  • Grey hair
  • Very light blonde hair
  • Some red hair
  • Very fine, lightly pigmented facial hair

The AAD notes that lasers cannot effectively target blonde, white, grey or red hair because these hairs contain too little suitable pigment.

Alternative methods may be discussed when the hair is unlikely to respond adequately.

Can laser hair reduction be performed on darker skin?

Yes, laser hair reduction can be performed on many darker skin tones when the device, wavelength, energy settings and cooling method are selected carefully.

Darker skin contains more melanin, so poorly chosen settings can also heat the surrounding skin. This can increase the risk of burns, blistering, dark marks or lighter patches.

The AAD advises that patients with darker skin choose a medical professional experienced in treating their skin tone.

Treatment planning may involve:

  • Skin-tone assessment
  • Conservative starting settings
  • Test spots where appropriate
  • Effective cooling
  • Careful monitoring of response
  • Strong sun-protection advice

Laser research has included many patients with darker phototypes, although the darkest skin types remain underrepresented in some clinical trials.

Does facial hair need a different treatment approach?

Facial hair—particularly on a woman’s chin, upper lip or jawline—can be influenced by hormones.

Laser may reduce suitable coarse facial hair, but new follicles can become active over time. Maintenance sessions may therefore be more important on the face than on some body areas.

Dr. Cheena Langer may ask about symptoms such as:

  • Irregular menstrual cycles
  • Sudden increase in facial hair
  • Acne
  • Scalp hair thinning
  • Recent weight changes
  • Current hormonal medicines

Laser can address the visible hair, but it does not by itself treat an underlying hormonal condition.

How should you prepare before laser hair reduction?

Preparation instructions can vary, but patients may be advised to:

  • Avoid tanning
  • Avoid sunless tanning products
  • Use broad-spectrum sunscreen
  • Avoid waxing, threading or plucking before treatment
  • Shave or trim the area as advised
  • Avoid bleaching the hair
  • Inform the clinic about new medicines
  • Avoid irritating skincare products when advised
  • Report active rashes, cuts or infections

The AAD recommends avoiding tanning and using broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher before treatment.

Do not apply perfume, deodorant, makeup or heavy creams to the treatment area unless the clinic says they are acceptable.

Should hair be shaved before treatment?

Shaving usually preserves the hair follicle under the skin while removing excess hair above the surface.

Waxing, threading, epilation and plucking remove the hair from the follicle, leaving less pigment for the laser to target.

Follow the clinic’s specific shaving instructions because the preferred timing may differ by area and skin sensitivity.

Do not shave irritated or infected skin without medical advice.

What happens during the procedure?

Before treatment:

  • The area is examined and cleaned
  • Protective eyewear is provided
  • Laser parameters are selected
  • Cooling may be used
  • Numbing cream may be considered for sensitive areas

During treatment, patients may feel warmth, pinpricks or a sensation similar to a light rubber-band snap. Treatment time depends on the size of the area; a small facial area may take minutes, while legs or the back take longer.

The operator observes the skin response and adjusts treatment only when medically appropriate.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
Is laser hair reduction painful?

The sensation varies according to:

  • Treatment area
  • Hair thickness
  • Skin sensitivity
  • Energy settings
  • Cooling system
  • Individual pain tolerance

Most patients describe temporary warmth, pinpricks or a mild snapping sensation.

Sensitive areas may feel more uncomfortable than the arms or legs.

Comfort varies between patients, so complete painlessness cannot be guaranteed.

Two locations in Jammu

Laser hair reduction is confirmed at both Karan Nagar and Paloura.

Reduce the cycle of shaving, waxing and recurrent irritation—book a laser hair reduction consultation with Dr. Cheena Langer in Jammu.

value.heading: How care is planned
value.body:
• Assessment comes before treatment selection.
  • Options, limitations, aftercare and expected timelines are explained.
  • The plan is adapted to diagnosis, skin type and medical history.

items.question: Is there downtime after treatment?
items.answer:
Most people can return to routine activities after laser hair reduction.

Temporary redness and swelling around the follicles are common and may resemble mild sunburn. These effects commonly settle within a few hours or days.

Patients should follow the clinic’s advice regarding:

  • Exercise
  • Heat exposure
  • Hot showers
  • Swimming
  • Makeup
  • Deodorant
  • Active skincare ingredients
  • Sun exposure

items.question: What aftercare is recommended?
items.answer:
After treatment, patients may be advised to:

  • Apply a cool compress if needed
  • Use a gentle moisturiser
  • Avoid rubbing or scratching
  • Avoid direct sunlight
  • Apply sunscreen regularly
  • Avoid tanning beds
  • Pause irritating products temporarily
  • Avoid excessive heat when advised
  • Follow prescribed aftercare
  • Contact the clinic for unexpected blistering or severe pain

AAD guidance emphasises sun avoidance and adherence to the dermatologist’s aftercare instructions.

items.question: What side effects are possible?
items.answer:
Common temporary effects include:

  • Redness
  • Swelling
  • Warmth
  • Tenderness
  • Mild itching
  • Follicular bumps

Less common complications may include:

  • Blistering
  • Burns
  • Infection
  • Scarring
  • Cold-sore reactivation
  • Darkening of the skin
  • Lightening of the skin

These risks increase when unsuitable settings are used or treatment is performed on recently tanned skin.

A systematic review also identified paradoxical hair stimulation as an uncommon potential complication, seen mainly around facial and neck areas.

items.question: How soon will results be visible?
items.answer:
Some treated hairs may shed during the days or weeks following a session.

After each treatment, patients may notice:

  • Slower regrowth
  • Fewer hairs
  • Finer hair
  • Softer hair
  • Patchier regrowth
  • Less frequent shaving

Results vary according to hair colour, thickness, treatment area, skin tone, laser type and individual biology.

The full response should be judged after a properly spaced treatment course rather than immediately after one session.

items.question: Will maintenance sessions be needed?
items.answer:
Some patients remain satisfied for long periods after completing a course, while others develop gradual regrowth.

Maintenance may be needed because:

  • Dormant follicles become active
  • Hormonal patterns continue
  • Facial hair is hormone-sensitive
  • Some follicles were not fully disabled
  • New hair develops with age or medical changes

The AAD notes that maintenance laser sessions may be needed when hair regrows.

items.question: Can laser treat ingrown hairs and razor bumps?
items.answer:
Reducing coarse hair can help some patients who repeatedly develop irritation, ingrown hairs or razor bumps after shaving.

However, acne-like bumps may sometimes represent:

  • Folliculitis
  • Pseudofolliculitis
  • Acne
  • Infection
  • Skin irritation

A dermatologist should confirm the diagnosis before assuming every bump is caused by ingrown hair.

items.question: When should treatment be postponed?
items.answer:
Treatment may need to be delayed when there is:

  • Recent tanning
  • Sunburn
  • Active skin infection
  • Open wounds
  • Significant irritation
  • Active herpes in the area
  • Recent use of certain medicines
  • An uncontrolled skin condition
  • Pregnancy-related clinic restrictions
  • Inability to follow sun protection

Always inform the clinic about pregnancy, breastfeeding, recent procedures and prescription medicines before treatment.

introduction: Dermatologist-led assessment and personalised care for laser tattoo removal, available at Karan Nagar and Paloura Chowk.

value.heading: What is laser tattoo removal?
value.body:
Laser tattoo removal uses short pulses of concentrated light to target tattoo pigment beneath the skin.

When an appropriate laser wavelength reaches the ink:

  • The pigment absorbs the laser energy
  • The ink breaks into smaller particles
  • The surrounding immune system gradually clears some of those particles
  • The tattoo becomes lighter over successive sessions

The laser does not physically pull ink out during the appointment. Much of the fading occurs gradually after treatment as the body processes fragmented pigment.

value.heading: What is a Q-switched Nd:YAG laser?
value.body:
A Q-switched Nd:YAG laser delivers very short, high-energy pulses designed to target selected tattoo pigments while limiting unnecessary heating of the surrounding skin.

Different wavelengths from this laser family may be used for different colours. Published reviews have evaluated Q-switched Nd:YAG treatment for black and coloured tattoos across different skin phototypes, while also noting that long-term evidence and treatment standardisation remain limited.

Q-switched Nd:YAG technology is listed as available within the Aastha Skin Centre machine inventory. The device’s manufacturer, exact wavelengths and regulatory status should not be claimed until supporting records are available.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Why are several sessions required?

Tattoo ink is deposited in layers within the deeper skin. Trying to destroy all the pigment in one appointment would increase the risk of burns, wounds, pigment changes and scarring.

Several sessions are needed because:

  • Only part of the pigment can be treated safely at one time
  • Different ink depths respond differently
  • The skin requires time to heal
  • The body needs time to clear fragmented pigment
  • Some colours need different laser wavelengths
  • Dense or layered tattoos contain more pigment

Laser treatments are therefore spaced several weeks apart. The exact interval depends on healing, tattoo characteristics and the patient’s skin response.

Can a tattoo be removed completely?

Sometimes substantial clearance is possible, but complete removal cannot be guaranteed.

Possible outcomes include:

  • Major fading
  • Partial removal
  • Enough lightening for a cover-up tattoo
  • Residual pigment
  • A faint “ghost” outline
  • Uneven clearance between colours
  • Visible pre-existing tattoo scarring

FDA guidance states that complete removal may take many treatments and may not be achievable in some cases.

The goal should be agreed before treatment: complete removal where realistically possible, substantial fading or preparation for a cover-up.

Which tattoos are easier to remove?

Response depends on several interacting factors.

Tattoos may respond more readily when they are:

  • Black or dark blue
  • Older
  • Less densely packed with ink
  • Amateur rather than heavily layered professional tattoos
  • Located in an area with good circulation
  • Free from significant pre-existing scarring

Dark blue and black pigments are generally easier to target than several bright or pale colours.

Even a small tattoo may require multiple sessions if the pigment is dense or deeply placed.

Which tattoos are harder to remove?

Treatment can be more difficult when the tattoo is:

  • Multicoloured
  • Recently applied
  • Professionally and densely layered
  • A cover-up over an older tattoo
  • Scarred
  • Located on the hands, feet or distant extremities
  • Made with resistant pigments
  • Cosmetic permanent makeup
  • White, beige or flesh-coloured
  • Associated with an inflammatory or allergic reaction

Published reviews note that professional and multicoloured tattoos may be particularly time-consuming and can leave residual pigment despite repeated treatment.

Which tattoo colours respond best?

Tattoo colour matters because different pigments absorb different wavelengths of light.

In general:

  • Black and dark blue: often respond more predictably
  • Red: may respond to a different wavelength from black
  • Green: can be more resistant and may require another laser wavelength
  • Yellow: often difficult to remove
  • White, beige and flesh tones: may darken unexpectedly
  • Mixed colours: may need more than one wavelength or treatment approach

The FDA notes that green, red and yellow can be more difficult than dark blue and black.

Not every tattoo colour responds equally; suitability depends on pigment and the available wavelength.

Can cosmetic tattoos and permanent makeup be removed?

Selected cosmetic tattoos may be treatable, including:

  • Eyebrow tattoos
  • Microblading pigment
  • Permanent eyeliner
  • Lip-liner tattoos
  • Scalp-micropigmentation areas

However, cosmetic pigment requires additional caution.

White, beige, red-brown and flesh-coloured inks may contain compounds that darken after laser exposure. What begins as a pale eyebrow or lip pigment can temporarily or permanently turn grey or black.

A test spot and staged plan may therefore be considered before treating a large cosmetic tattoo.

Can microblading be removed?

Microblading is a form of cosmetic tattooing in which pigment is placed into the skin to simulate eyebrow hairs.

Its response depends on:

  • Pigment composition
  • Colour
  • Depth
  • Number of previous sessions
  • Scarring
  • Skin tone
  • Whether pigments have changed colour over time

Some pigments can darken during initial laser treatment. A medical assessment and possible test spot are particularly important before treating eyebrow microblading.

Can a tattoo be lightened for a cover-up?

Yes. Some patients do not need complete tattoo removal.

Laser treatment may be used to:

  • Reduce the darkness of an old tattoo
  • Lighten dense sections
  • Reduce an outline
  • Make a future cover-up design easier
  • Improve the available colour options for a tattoo artist

The number of sessions needed for cover-up preparation may be lower than the number required for maximal removal.

The tattoo artist should usually wait until the treated skin has fully healed and the final degree of fading can be assessed.

Is laser tattoo removal suitable for Indian skin?

Laser tattoo removal can be performed on Indian and other medium-to-deep skin tones, but there is a greater need to protect the skin’s natural pigment.

Possible pigment-related effects include:

  • Temporary darkening
  • Temporary lightening
  • Prolonged uneven colour
  • Rare permanent pigment change
  • More visible post-inflammatory marks

Longer-wavelength Q-switched Nd:YAG treatment has historically been used in deeper skin tones, but conservative settings, suitable intervals and test treatment may still be needed.

Tattoo removal carries pigment-change risks, particularly in darker skin, so careful assessment is important.

What affects the number of sessions?

The treatment course may depend on:

  • Tattoo size
  • Number of colours
  • Ink density
  • Ink depth
  • Professional or amateur application
  • Cover-up layers
  • Tattoo location
  • Patient’s skin tone
  • Age of the tattoo
  • Existing scarring
  • Immune response
  • Healing between treatments
  • Desired endpoint

No online calculator can predict the exact number of appointments with certainty.

FDA guidance states that treatment duration depends on factors such as tattoo size and colour, and that some tattoos may never clear completely.

How does Dr. Cheena Langer assess a tattoo?

A consultation may include:

  • Examining the tattoo’s size and location
  • Recording each visible colour
  • Reviewing whether it is amateur, professional or cosmetic
  • Checking for cover-up layers
  • Assessing scars or raised areas
  • Examining the surrounding skin tone
  • Asking about itching, swelling or tattoo reactions
  • Reviewing previous laser or removal treatments
  • Checking medicines and medical history
  • Discussing complete removal versus lightening
  • Explaining likely sessions and limitations
  • Considering a test spot

The consultation should also identify moles, suspicious growths or inflammatory reactions hidden within the tattoo.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
Why must moles inside a tattoo be checked?

Tattoo pigment can make it harder to notice changes in a mole or other skin growth.

Before laser treatment, the dermatologist may examine:

  • Moles
  • Freckles
  • Raised growths
  • Bleeding areas

Non-healing sores

Irregular pigmentation

A suspicious lesion may need dermoscopy or biopsy before tattoo-removal treatment continues. The AAD recommends dermatologist assessment because skin spots revealed during removal may require investigation.

Surgical excision

A small tattoo may sometimes be cut out and the skin stitched together. This produces a surgical scar and is not suitable for every size or location.

Dermabrasion

The skin surface is mechanically abraded. Results can be unpredictable, and pigment may remain.

Ablative laser treatment

The upper skin layers are removed rather than selectively targeting only tattoo pigment. This can involve greater recovery and scarring risk.

The FDA notes that these methods are now less commonly used because outcomes are variable and unwanted cosmetic effects may be greater.

No. Laser tattoo removal targets ink, not the scar created when the tattoo was originally placed.

A tattoo may already contain:

  • Raised scar tissue
  • Depressed areas
  • Textural change
  • Needle-related injury
  • Keloid formation

As the pigment fades, pre-existing scarring may become more visible.

Separate scar treatment may be discussed after the tattoo-removal course and complete skin healing.

Dermatologist-led consultation

Treatment planning is provided under Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist.

Tattoo and skin are assessed together

Colour, ink density, scarring, skin tone and suspicious growths are reviewed before treatment.

Q-switched Nd:YAG technology is recorded in the clinic inventory, while unsupported brand and regulatory claims remain excluded.

Care for Indian skin tones

Treatment parameters are selected with attention to post-inflammatory pigmentation and loss of natural skin colour.

Realistic expectations

Patients are counselled that several sessions are required and complete clearance cannot be guaranteed.

Need help choosing?

Tattoo removal is a gradual treatment—not a one-session eraser

items.question: What happens during a laser tattoo-removal session?
items.answer:
A typical appointment may involve:

  • Confirming the tattoo and treatment area
  • Taking standardised photographs
  • Cleaning the skin
  • Covering nearby sensitive areas
  • Providing appropriate eye protection
  • Applying anaesthesia when indicated
  • Selecting suitable treatment parameters
  • Delivering laser pulses over the planned area
  • Cooling and examining the skin
  • Applying a dressing or aftercare product
  • Providing written instructions

A temporary white or frosted appearance can occur immediately after laser pulses because of a rapid reaction within the skin.

items.question: Is laser tattoo removal painful?
items.answer:
Tattoo removal can be uncomfortable or painful.

Patients commonly describe sensations such as:

  • Repeated rubber-band snaps
  • Stinging
  • Heat
  • Pinpricks
  • Burning
  • Tenderness after treatment

The FDA and AAD both note that numbing cream or local anaesthetic may be used to reduce discomfort.

The website should not promise painless tattoo removal.

items.question: What pain-control options may be used?
items.answer:
Depending on the tattoo and patient, comfort measures may include:

  • Cooling
  • Topical anaesthetic
  • Local-anaesthetic injection
  • Treatment in smaller sections
  • Pauses during treatment

Patients should not apply high-strength numbing cream purchased online without medical guidance.

The FDA has warned about some high-concentration topical anaesthetic products marketed for tattooing and laser procedures because excessive absorption can cause seizures, irregular heart rhythm and breathing problems.

items.question: Is there downtime after treatment?
items.answer:
Patients can often continue ordinary non-strenuous activities, but the treated skin needs time to heal.

Temporary effects may include:

  • Redness
  • Swelling
  • Tenderness
  • Pinpoint bleeding
  • Blistering
  • Crusting
  • Bruising
  • Temporary darkening
  • Temporary lightening
  • Itching during healing

These reactions vary according to the tattoo, settings, treatment area and individual skin response.

items.question: Is blistering normal after tattoo removal?
items.answer:
Small blisters can occur after laser tattoo removal.

Patients should:

  • Avoid deliberately bursting blisters
  • Keep the area clean
  • Follow the prescribed dressing plan
  • Avoid picking crusts
  • Contact the clinic if blistering is extensive
  • Seek review for increasing pain, pus or spreading redness

Large blisters, severe pain, skin breakdown or signs of infection require medical assessment.

items.question: What aftercare is recommended?
items.answer:
Clinic-specific instructions take priority. General aftercare may include:

  • Keep the area clean
  • Apply the recommended ointment or moisturiser
  • Cover the area when instructed
  • Avoid scratching and picking
  • Avoid swimming until the skin heals
  • Avoid tight friction over the area
  • Avoid waxing or shaving damaged skin
  • Avoid strong exfoliating products
  • Protect the area from sunlight
  • Attend the scheduled review

The AAD advises following wound-care instructions and protecting treated skin from the sun during recovery.

items.question: Why is sun protection important?
items.answer:
A recent tan increases the amount of melanin competing with tattoo pigment for laser energy.

Sun exposure before or after treatment may increase the risk of:

  • Burns
  • Hyperpigmentation
  • Hypopigmentation
  • Delayed healing
  • Uneven results

Patients may be advised to cover the treated area with opaque clothing and use suitable sunscreen after the skin surface has healed. The AAD recommends protecting treated skin from sunlight for an extended period after tattoo-removal treatment.

introduction: Dermatologist-led assessment and personalised care for lichen planus, available at Karan Nagar and Paloura Chowk.

value.heading: What is lichen planus?
value.body:
Lichen planus is an inflammatory disorder in which immune activity targets cells within the skin or mucous membranes.

It may affect:

  • Skin
  • Inside the mouth
  • Lips
  • Scalp and hair follicles
  • Fingernails and toenails
  • Vulva and vagina
  • Penis
  • Other genital skin

Some patients develop disease at only one site, while others have involvement of several areas.

value.heading: What causes lichen planus?
value.body:
The exact cause is not completely understood.

Lichen planus is believed to develop when the immune system mistakenly attacks cells in the skin or mucous membranes. Why this begins in one person and not another is often unclear.

Possible contributing factors may include:

  • Genetic susceptibility
  • Immune dysregulation
  • Skin injury
  • Certain medicines
  • Contact allergy in selected oral lesions
  • Associated infection or another medical condition in particular patients

A trigger is not identified in many cases.

value.heading: What is oral lichen planus?
value.body:
Oral lichen planus affects the inside of the mouth.

It may involve:

  • Inner cheeks
  • Gums
  • Tongue
  • Roof of the mouth
  • Lips

Some patients develop only painless white lacy lines. Others develop redness, burning, raw areas or painful ulcers that interfere with eating and oral hygiene.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Is lichen planus contagious?

No. Lichen planus is not contagious.

It cannot spread through:

  • Touching
  • Sharing towels
  • Food
  • Kissing
  • Sexual contact
  • Swimming
  • Living in the same household

Lichen planus is an inflammatory condition rather than a bacterial, fungal or viral infection that passes from one person to another.

Is genital lichen planus a sexually transmitted infection?

No. Genital lichen planus is not an STI.

However, genital disease can cause soreness, burning, erosions and pain during sexual activity. It may resemble infection, allergy, lichen sclerosus or another genital condition, so diagnosis should be confirmed before treatment.

Can medicines cause a lichen-planus-like rash?

Yes. Some medicines can produce a lichenoid drug eruption, which resembles lichen planus.

The rash may begin weeks or months after a medicine was started. A careful review of prescription medicines, non-prescription drugs and supplements is therefore part of assessment.

Patients should not stop an important prescribed medicine independently. The suspected relationship should be discussed with the dermatologist and the original prescribing doctor.

What does lichen planus look like on the skin?

Classic skin lichen planus may produce:

  • Small, raised bumps
  • Flat-topped lesions
  • Purple, violet, brown or grey colour
  • Fine white lines on the surface
  • Intense itching
  • Groups of closely packed bumps
  • Thickened plaques
  • Ring-shaped lesions
  • Dark marks after healing

The wrists, ankles, lower back and legs are commonly affected, although lesions can appear elsewhere.

How does lichen planus appear on Indian skin?

On medium-to-deep Indian skin tones, lichen planus may appear:

  • Dark brown
  • Purple-brown
  • Violet
  • Grey
  • Nearly black
  • Less visibly red than expected

After the active bumps settle, dark post-inflammatory marks may remain for months or occasionally longer. These marks are more frequent and can be more noticeable in darker skin tones.

What are Wickham striae?

Wickham striae are fine white or grey lines seen across the surface of some lichen planus bumps or oral lesions.

They may create a:

  • Lacy pattern
  • Net-like pattern
  • Branching pattern
  • Fine white surface marking

Their presence can support the diagnosis, but they may be subtle or absent.

Can lichen planus develop after scratching or injury?

Yes. New lesions can sometimes develop along an area of skin injury, known as the Koebner phenomenon.

Possible triggers include:

  • Scratching
  • Cuts
  • Friction
  • Burns
  • Surgical scars
  • Tattoos
  • Repeated rubbing

Reducing scratching and protecting inflamed skin can help limit further injury.

Does skin lichen planus clear naturally?

Skin lichen planus may improve without treatment, particularly when disease is mild and limited.

Many cutaneous cases clear over approximately one to two years, although the timeframe varies. Dark marks may remain after the raised lesions have resolved. Oral, genital, scalp and nail lichen planus can last longer and may need active treatment or monitoring.

What are the types of oral lichen planus?

Reticular oral lichen planus

This form causes white lacy lines or small white patches and may produce little or no discomfort.

Erosive oral lichen planus

This form causes raw, red, ulcerated or painful areas.

Atrophic oral lichen planus

The lining appears thin, inflamed and sensitive.

Plaque-like oral lichen planus

Thicker white patches may develop and need differentiation from other oral conditions.

Different patterns can occur together.

What symptoms can oral lichen planus cause?

Possible symptoms include:

  • Burning
  • Stinging
  • Mouth soreness
  • Pain while eating
  • Sensitivity to spicy food
  • Sensitivity to acidic food
  • Bleeding gums
  • Pain during brushing
  • Painful ulcers
  • Altered taste
  • Dry or uncomfortable mouth

Symptoms may fluctuate, with periods of improvement followed by flare-ups.

Does oral lichen planus increase the risk of oral cancer?

Oral lichen planus carries a small but clinically important potential for malignant change, particularly in persistent red, erosive or ulcerated disease.

Published estimates vary because studies use different diagnostic criteria and may include oral lichenoid lesions that are not identical to true lichen planus. Reviews using strict criteria have reported lower transformation rates than broader studies, but regular examination remains appropriate.

A persistent ulcer, lump, hardened area, unexplained bleeding or changing lesion should be examined promptly and may require biopsy.

Which oral changes require prompt reassessment?

Arrange timely review for:

  • An ulcer that does not heal
  • A lump or thickened area
  • Increasing pain
  • Unexplained bleeding
  • A change in colour or surface
  • Difficulty swallowing
  • Persistent hoarseness
  • Reduced tongue movement
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Enlarged neck lymph nodes

These changes do not automatically mean cancer, but they should not be attributed to routine lichen planus without examination.

Why are dental check-ups important?

Good dental and gum health can reduce additional irritation in an already sensitive mouth.

Patients with oral lichen planus may be advised to:

  • Brush gently twice daily
  • Use a soft toothbrush
  • Floss or use an appropriate interdental cleaner
  • Attend regular dental examinations
  • Have professional cleaning as advised
  • Address sharp teeth or poorly fitting dental appliances
  • Avoid toothpaste that repeatedly burns or irritates

Ongoing review by a dermatologist, dentist or oral-medicine clinician may be appropriate according to the disease pattern.

Which foods may irritate oral lichen planus?

During an active flare, discomfort may worsen with:

  • Spicy food
  • Acidic food
  • Citrus fruit
  • Very salty food
  • Hard or crunchy food
  • Very hot drinks
  • Alcohol
  • Tobacco

Patients do not need to remove every item permanently. The goal is to avoid foods that repeatedly cause pain while maintaining a balanced diet.

items.heading: Additional care and practical advice
items.body:
Can dental materials trigger a lichenoid reaction?

Some oral lichenoid lesions may develop next to a dental material or another local irritant.

Assessment may consider:

  • Dental fillings
  • Metals
  • Dental appliances
  • Toothpaste ingredients
  • Mouthwash
  • Cinnamon or flavouring agents
  • Repeated mechanical trauma

Removal or replacement of dental work should not be undertaken without coordinated dental and dermatological assessment.

What is lichen planopilaris?

Lichen planopilaris is lichen planus affecting the scalp hair follicles.

It can cause:

  • Scalp itching
  • Burning
  • Tenderness
  • Redness around hair follicles
  • Perifollicular scale
  • Patchy hair loss
  • Loss of follicular openings
  • Permanent scarring alopecia

Unlike alopecia areata, lichen planopilaris can destroy follicles permanently. Treatment aims primarily to stop inflammatory progression and preserve remaining hair.

Why is early diagnosis of lichen planopilaris important?

Hair that has already been lost because of follicular scarring may not regrow.

Early treatment may:

  • Reduce itching and burning
  • Control scalp inflammation
  • Slow extension of bald areas
  • Protect follicles that remain
  • Reduce permanent hair loss

A painful, burning or scaly area of scalp hair loss should therefore be assessed without waiting for it to become large.

How is lichen planopilaris different from alopecia areata?

  • Is a scarring alopecia
  • May cause scalp burning or tenderness
  • Produces inflammation and scale around follicles
  • Can permanently destroy follicles
  • Often requires biopsy when uncertain
  • Is usually non-scarring
  • Commonly produces smooth bald patches
  • Preserves follicular openings
  • Allows potential regrowth
  • May affect nails, eyebrows or beard

The consultation can include the skin, mouth, scalp, nails and genital symptoms rather than treating only the most visible rash.

Lichen planus is distinguished from eczema, psoriasis, fungal infection, lupus, lichenoid drug eruption and other similar conditions.

Skin biopsy is available at both branches for selected uncertain, scarring or changing lesions.

Scalp and nail lichen planus can cause permanent damage, making timely diagnosis especially important.

Treatment is planned under Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist.

Persistent erosive mucosal disease is followed for symptom control, scarring and suspicious changes.

General dermatology consultation is available at both Karan Nagar and Paloura.

Additional cost depends on:

  • Body area affected
  • Topical medicine
  • Mouth rinse, gel or paste
  • Corticosteroid injections
  • Skin, scalp, nail or oral biopsy
  • Blood tests
  • Treatment of secondary infection
  • Systemic medicine and monitoring
  • Dental or oral-medicine review
  • External phototherapy
  • Follow-up after the included 10-day period

Skin-only lichen planus generally requires a different plan from erosive oral disease, progressive nail damage or scarring scalp involvement.

value.heading: How care is planned
value.body:
• Assessment comes before treatment selection.
  • Options, limitations, aftercare and expected timelines are explained.
  • The plan is adapted to diagnosis, skin type and medical history.

items.question: Can lichen planus affect the nails?
items.answer:
Yes. Nail lichen planus may affect one, several or all nails.

Possible changes include:

  • Longitudinal ridges
  • Roughness
  • Thinning
  • Splitting
  • Loss of shine
  • Crumbling
  • Separation
  • Reduced nail growth
  • Scarring beneath or around the nail
  • Permanent nail loss

Early treatment matters because established nail scarring may be irreversible.

items.question: Is every rough or damaged nail caused by lichen planus?
items.answer:
No.

Similar nail changes can result from:

  • Fungal infection
  • Psoriasis
  • Trauma
  • Eczema
  • Alopecia areata
  • Repeated manicure damage
  • Nutritional or systemic disease
  • Other inflammatory nail disorders

Nail clippings, fungal testing or biopsy may be considered when the diagnosis remains uncertain.

items.question: What is genital lichen planus?
items.answer:
Genital lichen planus can affect the vulva, vagina, penis or surrounding genital skin.

Possible symptoms include:

  • Itching
  • Burning
  • Soreness
  • Pain
  • Red or darker patches
  • White lacy markings
  • Raw erosions
  • Bleeding
  • Pain during sexual activity
  • Scarring

Genital disease may require prolonged treatment and monitoring because erosive inflammation can damage sensitive tissue.

items.question: Can genital lichen planus cause scarring?
items.answer:
Yes. Persistent erosive genital disease may lead to:

  • Adhesions
  • Narrowing
  • Altered anatomy
  • Pain during intercourse
  • Urinary discomfort
  • Vaginal narrowing in severe cases
  • Foreskin or penile scarring

Early assessment and consistent treatment can help reduce progressive inflammation and scarring.

items.question: What is vulvovaginal-gingival syndrome?
items.answer:
Some patients develop erosive lichen planus involving both:

  • The mouth or gums
  • The vulva or vagina

This pattern may be referred to as vulvovaginal-gingival syndrome.

Patients with persistent oral lichen planus should mention genital soreness, and patients with genital disease should report mouth ulcers or gum inflammation.

items.question: Can men develop genital lichen planus?
items.answer:
Yes.

Penile lichen planus may produce:

  • Ring-shaped patches
  • Purple, brown or white lesions
  • Itching
  • Soreness
  • Erosions
  • Scarring

It must be distinguished from fungal infection, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus, fixed drug eruption and sexually transmitted infections.

items.question: Can children develop lichen planus?
items.answer:
Yes, although lichen planus is less common in children than adults.

Children may develop:

  • Skin bumps
  • Oral lesions
  • Nail changes
  • Scalp involvement
  • Dark marks after healing

Treatment should consider the child’s age, body area, disease severity and risk of long-term scarring. Painful procedures or systemic medicines require careful risk–benefit assessment.

value.body:
Consult Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist, for diagnosis-led melasma treatment at Aastha Skin & Dermato-Cosmetic Centre in Jammu.

Melasma commonly causes brown or grey-brown facial patches, especially on the cheeks, forehead, upper lip and jawline. It is a chronic condition that can improve with treatment but may return when triggers remain active.

Melasma and pigmentation treatment are available at both Karan Nagar and Paloura.

value.heading: What is melasma?
value.body:
Melasma is an acquired pigmentation condition that produces flat, irregular brown or grey-brown patches, usually on sun-exposed areas of the face. It does not normally cause pain, scaling or infection, but its appearance may affect confidence and emotional wellbeing.

Melasma is different from:

  • Post-acne marks
  • Freckles
  • Sun spots
  • Allergic pigmentation
  • Lichen planus pigmentosus
  • Acquired dermal macular pigmentation
  • Pigmentation caused by medicines or cosmetics

A dermatologist should confirm the diagnosis before treatment because these conditions may look similar but respond differently.

value.heading: What causes melasma?
value.body:
Melasma does not have one single cause. It appears to develop through a combination of genetic susceptibility, pigment-cell activity, ultraviolet radiation, visible light and hormonal influences.

Common triggers or contributing factors include:

  • Sun exposure
  • Visible light
  • Pregnancy
  • Hormonal medicines
  • Genetic tendency
  • Heat exposure
  • Irritating skincare
  • Certain cosmetics
  • Some medicines
  • Previous inflammation

Melasma is not caused by poor hygiene and cannot be removed by scrubbing the skin.

value.heading: How does Dr. Cheena Langer assess melasma?
value.body:
A melasma consultation may include:

  • Examining the pattern and colour of the pigmentation
  • Assessing whether the pigment appears superficial, deep or mixed
  • Reviewing when it began
  • Asking about pregnancy and hormonal medicines
  • Reviewing previous creams, peels and laser procedures
  • Checking for acne, eczema or irritation
  • Assessing sunlight, visible-light and heat exposure
  • Reviewing current skincare and cosmetics
  • Looking for another pigmentary disorder
  • Discussing treatment expectations and recurrence

A dermatoscope or Wood’s lamp may be used when clinically helpful. Not every patient requires laboratory investigations.

value.heading: How is melasma treated?
value.body:
Melasma treatment usually combines photoprotection, topical medication, gentle skincare and maintenance. Procedures may be added for selected patients when first-line treatment is insufficient or when the diagnosis and skin type make them appropriate.

A personalised plan may include:

  • Broad-spectrum sunscreen
  • Visible-light protection
  • Prescription depigmenting creams
  • Gentle moisturisers and cleansers
  • Chemical peels
  • Tranexamic-acid-based treatment in selected patients
  • Q-switched laser or laser toning in selected cases
  • Maintenance treatment

No single cream, peel or laser is suitable for every patient.

items.heading: Types, options and detailed guidance
items.body:
Where does melasma usually appear?

Melasma most commonly develops on:

  • Cheeks
  • Forehead
  • Nose
  • Upper lip
  • Chin
  • Jawline

The patches often appear on both sides of the face in a relatively symmetrical pattern.

Less commonly, pigmentation may involve the neck or forearms. An unusual distribution may require evaluation for another pigmentation disorder.

Can pregnancy cause melasma?

Yes. Hormonal changes during pregnancy can trigger or worsen melasma in susceptible individuals.

Patients should inform the dermatologist when they:

  • Are pregnant
  • Are breastfeeding
  • Are trying to conceive
  • Use hormonal contraception
  • Take hormonal treatment

Some melasma medicines and oral treatments are unsuitable during pregnancy. Treatment during this period may therefore focus on gentle skincare and strict photoprotection.

Why does melasma keep coming back?

Melasma commonly recurs because the underlying tendency remains even after the pigmentation improves.

Recurrence may follow:

  • Sun exposure
  • Visible-light exposure
  • Heat
  • Hormonal changes
  • Stopping maintenance treatment
  • Skin irritation
  • Inconsistent sunscreen use

Current consensus approaches treat melasma as a condition that often requires ongoing control and maintenance rather than a one-time permanent cure.

Why is sunscreen essential for melasma?

Ultraviolet radiation can darken melasma, and visible light can also contribute to pigmentation, especially in medium-to-deep skin tones.

The American Academy of Dermatology recommends daily sun protection as a central part of melasma care.

Patients may be advised to use:

  • Broad-spectrum sunscreen
  • SPF 30 or higher
  • A tinted product containing iron oxides where appropriate
  • Hats, umbrellas or physical shade
  • Regular reapplication
  • Protection during travel and outdoor work

A prospective randomised study found that visible-light-protective tinted sunscreen provided greater protection against seasonal melasma worsening than an untinted comparator.

What creams may be prescribed?

Depending on the diagnosis, severity, skin sensitivity and pregnancy status, treatment may include agents such as:

  • Hydroquinone
  • Retinoids
  • Azelaic acid
  • Cysteamine
  • Kojic-acid-containing preparations
  • Tranexamic-acid-containing topical treatment
  • Carefully supervised combination creams

These medicines may cause dryness, redness or irritation. The strength, duration and combination should be selected by a qualified medical professional.

Unsupervised long-term use of strong depigmenting or steroid-mixed creams may damage the skin and worsen pigmentation.

Can chemical peels help melasma?

Chemical peels may be used as an additional treatment for selected patients. They work by producing controlled exfoliation of superficial skin layers.

Possible peel options vary according to:

  • Skin tone
  • Melasma depth
  • Skin sensitivity
  • Active irritation
  • Previous treatments
  • Pigmentation risk

Peels are generally used as an adjunct rather than the foundation of treatment. Procedures are not recommended as first-line therapy for every mild case.

Possible temporary effects include:

  • Redness
  • Dryness
  • Peeling
  • Sensitivity
  • Temporary darkening
  • Post-inflammatory pigmentation

Stronger peeling does not automatically produce better results.

Can laser treatment help melasma?

Laser or energy-based treatment may be considered for selected or resistant melasma, but it is not automatically the first treatment.

Possible options may include:

  • Q-switched laser
  • Low-fluence laser toning
  • Other carefully selected procedures

Laser treatment can sometimes improve pigmentation but may also cause rebound darkening, uneven lightening or recurrence. Current consensus recommendations reserve procedural treatments for appropriate cases and combine them with photoprotection and medical therapy.

Patients should not be promised permanent clearance or instant whitening.

What is laser toning?

Laser toning usually refers to repeated low-fluence Q-switched laser sessions performed at controlled settings.

It may be considered when:

  • The diagnosis has been confirmed
  • Topical treatment has been insufficient
  • The skin type and pigment pattern are suitable
  • The patient understands recurrence and risks

Potential complications include:

  • Irritation
  • Rebound pigmentation
  • Mottled lighter patches
  • Uneven tone
  • Temporary sensitivity

The number of sessions and treatment settings must be individualised.

Can tranexamic acid be used for melasma?

Tranexamic acid may be used topically, through selected procedures or orally in carefully screened patients.

Systematic reviews and expert consensus suggest oral tranexamic acid can improve melasma in selected patients, but it requires medical evaluation because of potential clotting risks and contraindications.

Before considering oral treatment, the doctor may review:

  • Previous blood clots
  • Clotting disorders
  • Smoking history
  • Hormonal contraception
  • Pregnancy
  • Cardiovascular risk
  • Family history
  • Current medicines

Patients should not self-medicate with oral tranexamic acid for pigmentation.

Diagnosis before treatment

Melasma is distinguished from post-acne marks, freckles and deeper pigmentary disorders before selecting a cream, peel or laser.

Dermatologist-led care

Treatment is planned under Dr. Cheena Langer, MBBS, MD Dermatology, Consultant Dermatologist.

Professional focus in pigmentation

Dr. Cheena Langer’s verified professional record includes teaching and conference activity related to melasma and pigmentary disorders.

items.question: Is melasma treatment safe for Indian skin?
items.answer:
Yes, but Indian and other medium-to-deep skin tones can develop additional pigmentation after irritation, burns or aggressive procedures.

Safer treatment planning prioritises:

  • Correct diagnosis
  • Gentle skincare
  • Gradual treatment escalation
  • Careful procedure selection
  • Visible-light and sun protection
  • Early management of irritation
  • Maintenance treatment

A stronger laser or deeper peel is not automatically more effective and may increase the risk of post-inflammatory pigmentation.

items.question: How long does melasma treatment take?
items.answer:
Melasma usually improves gradually over weeks or months.

The timeline depends on:

  • Pigment depth
  • Duration of melasma
  • Skin type
  • Treatment selected
  • Trigger control
  • Sunscreen use
  • Skin sensitivity
  • Previous treatment
  • Individual response

Treatment should usually be reviewed after an appropriate period rather than changed every few days. Consensus recommendations commonly include reassessment after several weeks and continued maintenance after improvement.

items.question: Can melasma be cured permanently?
items.answer:
Melasma can often be lightened and controlled, but permanent cure cannot be guaranteed.

The realistic goals are to:

  • Reduce visible pigmentation
  • Prevent worsening
  • Improve evenness of tone
  • Identify triggers
  • Maintain results
  • Reduce recurrence

Patients should be cautious of treatments promising permanent removal in one sitting.

items.question: Which skincare habits can worsen melasma?
items.answer:
Melasma may worsen when the skin becomes irritated.

Avoid:

  • Harsh scrubs
  • Frequent bleaching
  • Undiluted lemon juice
  • Toothpaste
  • Strong acids bought online
  • Unlabelled fairness creams
  • Repeatedly changing active ingredients
  • Scratching or rubbing
  • Overuse of exfoliating products

The AAD advises using gentle products because burning or stinging can darken melasma.

items.question: Is heat a trigger for melasma?
items.answer:
Some patients report worsening with heat exposure, including cooking heat, hot environments or occupational exposure.

Heat may not affect every patient equally, but individuals who notice a consistent relationship should discuss practical trigger reduction with their dermatologist.

Sun protection remains essential even when heat appears to be an important trigger.
